content_en:
Confession: When BougeRV told me about its remote-controlled wagon with animated lighting, I called it in for a laugh, expecting to eviscerate it in a review. It’s ridiculous, to be sure. But the DuneRover also proved very capable, with enough torque to flatten hills even when carrying over 200 pounds of gear. It can also traverse soft sand that defeats conventional wagons.
This remote-controlled wagon is silly but so very useful
BougeRV’s DuneRover is so good on hills and sand that you’ll forgive the disco lights.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
As someone who regularly uses a variety of wagons to haul all sorts of gear, the DuneRover is an epiphany. But what BougeRV sent me was a Kickstarter prototype — and it shows.
Production units won’t ship until February 2027. So, what follows is less of a review and more a risk assessment for those considering backing the Kickstarter. That way, you can decide whether it makes sense to lock down early-bird pricing at $467, a claimed 48 percent discount off the eventual $899 list price. (Though I’ll wager it’ll always be sold for some kind of discount.)
Frankly, $500 isn’t outlandish for a wagon. Prices start at around $40 for a rickety model that will only last a few months, $300 for something durable from a reputable brand, and closer to $800 at the top end. And none of those wagons provides a motorized assist.
Let’s begin with the dumb stuff. The wagon has LED light bars on the back that are on by default and could come in handy at a campsite after dark. You can turn them off via the app, but you have to do it every time you restart the wagon. The default for a battery-powered device used primarily during the day should obviously be off.
Then there’s the remote control. I think I know what happened here. The product designers had a choice: route a cable through all the folding mechanisms that separate the motor from the handle or make it wireless. Wireless won, and then someone from marketing said, ‘Hey, I’ve got an idea!’
I mean, a remote-controlled wagon is so absurd that it’s kind of fun, and it brought a lot of joyful finger-pointing to onlookers during my testing. Maybe that’s enough?
The DuneRover is no joke for hauling gear. It’s fitted with two brushless geared motors, each producing up to 400W of output and up to 33Nm of torque. The wagon is activated by a trigger embedded in the handle that you press naturally when you pull the cart. Walk faster and the wagon will roll faster. Sometimes the wagon will lurch forward on that initial pull before settling into your walking rhythm. It’s not dangerous, it’s just unexpected. Release the trigger on the handle, and the wagon stops, even on an incline.
Pulling an oversized load weighing over 200 pounds up a 10 percent grade required a modicum of effort — but just a tenth of what it would have taken without the motor assist. Even on that steep incline, the wagon stops (with an inch or two of rollback) just as soon as I let go of the trigger. Repeated stopping and starting on slopes did, however, seem to confuse the DuneRover, occasionally causing the motors to become jerky as soon as I started walking again. A simple on/off resumed normal operation.
The motors also regulate speed when walking downhill with a heavy load. With the trigger held down, the controller did a good job monitoring changes in acceleration and countering the wagon’s speed to maintain my walking pace. When I stopped, so did the wagon, even on that 10 percent grade with a 200-plus pound load.
The motors aren’t powerful enough to haul that same load through soft sand, however. The oversized beach wheels performed much better in sand with loads weighing about half that, and should be excellent for families carrying a cooler, snacks, beach umbrella, toddler, and toys for a day at the beach.
I like that the DuneRover easily transformed depending on what I needed to haul. The sides can be unzipped and folded flat to convert the wagon into a cart for hauling oversized items or a senior dog. You can also unzip the sides but leave the straps connected to create more volume inside the wagon. I used this configuration a lot. Just know that you’ll want to bring a few bungee cords or cargo nets to keep everything securely in place.
My prototype suffered from intermittent rolling resistance with the motor off. The wagon would roll along fine for five or six feet, but then the wheels attached to the motors would brake, drag along the ground, and then release after a second or two. BougeRV assures me this isn’t something that would be exhibited by its production wagons. I ended up just leaving the motor on throughout my testing, even when I didn’t need it. The 82.14Wh battery was more than up to the challenge.
I used the DuneRover to move gear out of a beach house along the same route where I tested BougeRV’s original electric wagon. Six times I pulled the DuneRover along a path with 5 percent grade on one end and a 10 percent grade on the other. After six kilometers (3.73 miles) of soft sand, hard asphalt, wooden ramps, and gravel, the battery still showed a 74 percent charge. Not bad.
The removable battery features a bi-directional 100W USB-C port, making it a rather capable power bank. It can also charge from a 100W solar panel plugged into its XT-60 jack, thanks to a built-in MPPT solar controller. The battery in my prototype is not protected against rain, so I tested it in dry conditions, though BougeRV promises “full-vehicle IPX6-rated protection” in the production wagon.
The DuneRover is a beast at 59.5 pounds (27kg) with the battery and wheels installed. It’s also rather chunky when it folds. The quick-release front wheels can be removed if a flatter pack is required.
Overall, I’m impressed with the prototype DuneRover I tested — it’s capable, versatile, and proved to be an enormous help over the last few weeks of moving things between a holiday home, home, and adventure...

title_en: Common mistakes you should avoid when using foldable phones
title_fa: Common mistakes you should avoid when using foldable phones
excerpt_en: Foldable phones have unique durability concerns thanks to their moving parts and internal screens.
excerpt_fa: Foldable phones have unique durability concerns thanks to their moving parts and internal screens.
content_en:
Common mistakes you should avoid when using foldable phones
Your phone can fold in half, but your keys shouldn’t join it.
The most common mistake you should avoid when using foldable phones is dropping them. But that's common knowledge and doesn't make for a very exciting discussion. You're probably thinking about the inside foldable screen, where the most common way to damage it is closing it on something that shouldn't be there. Samsung's foldable care page warns that cards, coins or keys can scratch or even puncture a Galaxy foldable's inner display.
That seems straightforward enough; just make sure your car keys aren't sitting on top of your phone when you try to close it. But if you work a particularly dirty job or live near the beach, that complicates matters. You can't always spot dirt easily, and beach sand will find its way into absolutely anything.
Keep in mind that not all foldables are on equal footing. Some foldable screens are a bit softer and weaker than others. The Galaxy Z Fold8 and Fold8 Ultra, for instance, have an IP48 rating, whereas the new iPhone Duo boasts an IP68. The first digit describes the degree of protection against solid objects; a 4 means objects 1mm thick or larger can't enter, while 6 indicates a dust-tight device.
Treat the inner screen with care
A foldable's inner screen is far from a conventional slab-phone display. It has to fold, after all, so don't assume you can press on it as firmly as you would on a standard phone's outer glass. That includes actions you've probably done without thinking, like scratching a speck from the screen with your nail.
Another mistake is peeling off a factory-applied inner screen film because it looks like disposable shipping protection. This was surprisingly easy to do early on, but now the edges are tucked in and better hidden. Samsung highly recommends leaving these protective layers alone. On the flipside, don't stick an unapproved screen protector over a foldable display. These phones aren't like their slab cousins, so any old screen protector won't do. Only use a protector or stylus the manufacturer specifically lists as compatible with that model.
You don't have to baby a foldable phone, though it may seem that way coming from a traditional smartphone. These precautions just require you to be a little more particular when handling the folding screen. Avoid any concentrated force or closing it on anything other than open air.
What is the lifespan of a foldable phone?
There is no specific lifespan for foldables, though there are suggestions and indicators. For instance, we know that manufacturers test the hinges and screens by folding the phones between 200,000 and 500,000 times. If you open your phone 100 times a day, that would be 5 to 10 years.
However, that's not a guarantee. Samsung claimed the Galaxy Z Fold7's display remained functional after 500,000 folds in lab testing. Sounds pretty reassuring, but a controlled test doesn't mean the Fold7 would survive that many opens and closes throughout your daily life. In the past, Samsung's claim of 200,000 folds on the original Galaxy Fold fell short. When you hear figures tossed around, treat them as general benchmarks and marketing numbers.
Besides, it's far more useful to check for dirt before you close the phone than to count your folds each day. Don't push heavily on the display or use the wrong stylus. Use a soft cloth to clean marks on the screen instead of digging at them with your fingernail. And while the IP68 rating sounds great, Apple notes that the iPhone Duo's water and dust resistance may diminish with normal wear. Nothing lasts forever, but wear increases faster when moving parts are involved.

title_en: Can a MacBook handle heavy games? Here's what you should know
title_fa: Can a MacBook handle heavy games? Here's what you should know
excerpt_en: macOS is now a far healthier platform for gaming than it was just a few years ago, but it can't compete with Windows in many ways.
excerpt_fa: macOS is now a far healthier platform for gaming than it was just a few years ago, but it can't compete with Windows in many ways.
content_en:
Can a MacBook handle heavy games? Here's what you should know
The gap between Mac and PC is finally closing, but be careful before you pick a Mac as your primary gaming platform.
Macs have never exactly been gaming machines. For a long time, not only was the hardware lacking, but many developers never bothered to bring their titles to macOS. But the situation is different now with Apple silicon — the M-series chips are powerful, and there are new tools to easily port PC games to Mac.
But can a MacBook really handle demanding games? Technically, it can, but there are many other factors you should consider before choosing a Mac as your gaming machine. Yes, the gaming landscape on macOS is much better now than it was six years ago, but there's still a huge gap between Macs and Windows PCs.
What a MacBook can and can't handle
Thanks to Apple silicon, hardware is no longer a Mac's weak point. If you have one of the latest Macs, such as an M5 MacBook Pro, it will likely run most games well — even some big names you might not have expected. Apple lists Assassin's Creed Shadows, Dead Island 2 and Cyberpunk 2077 as some of the titles a Mac can run natively. The list of Mac-compatible games has been growing a lot, with more and more titles coming to macOS alongside their Windows versions.
And even if your favorite game doesn't have a macOS port, there may still be an alternative. Apple has created something called the Gaming Porting Toolkit, which helps developers port Windows games to macOS using native translations. While this tool is intended for developers, anyone can use it to run PC games on a Mac with just a few lines of code. I've been using it to run GTA V on my M4 Pro MacBook Pro, and the results are pretty solid; I can get a steady 60 frames per second with high graphics settings. It's not perfect and there are a few glitches here and there, but it works well overall for a game being translated in real-time.
If you're not sure which games your Mac can run, it's worth checking out MacGamingDB. This is a community-run website that provides compatibility details for thousands of titles, making it easy to quickly find out how your favorite game performs on a specific Mac model. It saves you a lot of time, since you don't have to download gigabytes of data just to find out the game doesn't work.
Which MacBook to buy, and when to look elsewhere
If you really want to game on a MacBook, the MacBook Pro is your best option. Even the base model with the M5 Pro chip and 24GB of RAM gives you enough power to run most modern games smoothly. If you need more, you can upgrade it with an M5 Max chip, which adds more RAM and a better GPU.
Of course, don't expect a MacBook Neo to perform the same as the latest MacBook Pro line. Both the MacBook Neo and the MacBook Air have less powerful processors and no internal fan, which makes them less suitable for running demanding games. They can still run some titles, but performance won't be ideal and you'll have to lower the resolution and graphics settings a bit.
But if you're serious about gaming, you should probably buy a PC instead. A Windows PC will likely cost you less for the same graphical power, and it will run all games natively without you having to worry about compatibility issues. You might also want to check out cloud gaming services like GeForce NOW or Xbox Cloud Gaming to stream games on your MacBook, so hardware won't be an issue. You just need a good internet connection.

title_en: Gemini Call for Me might tell your mom you’re running late
title_fa: Gemini Call for Me might tell your mom you’re running late
excerpt_en: Google may be expanding its "Call for Me" AI feature beyond business calls so you can use it to send messages to friends and family. Android Authority reports finding a "Gemini Calling" introductory screen in an APK teardown with examples that include "Call Mom and tell her I...
excerpt_fa: Google may be expanding its "Call for Me" AI feature beyond business calls so you can use it to send messages to friends and family. Android Authority reports finding a "Gemini Calling" introductory screen in an APK teardown with examples that include "Call Mom and tell her I...
content_en:
Google may be expanding its “Call for Me” AI feature beyond business calls so you can use it to send messages to friends and family. Android Authority reports finding a “Gemini Calling” introductory screen in an APK teardown with examples that include “Call Mom and tell her I will be 15 minutes late” and “Call John and ask if he is coming for dinner.”
Gemini Call for Me might tell your mom you’re running late
A rumored Android update would automate personal phone calls with Gemini AI.
A rumored Android update would automate personal phone calls with Gemini AI.
Based on those examples, even with this expansion, Gemini would likely be limited to basic, text message-like calls. While Google’s AI might not automate an entire catch-up phone call with your relatives, it could deliver quick messages to people who prefer a phone call, miss texts often, or even still have a landline phone.
Android Authority also says it found “granular permissions” for Gemini actions in individual apps, including what appear to be settings for phone call permissions. These settings would allow users to pick and choose which app capabilities they want to allow Gemini to access, potentially giving users an option to opt out of receiving incoming automated calls from Gemini. However, as Android Authority notes, it’s also possible Google might not publicly release this expansion or the granular Gemini app settings.

title_en: Mini PC vs. laptop: Which is better for your home office?
title_fa: Mini PC vs. laptop: Which is better for your home office?
excerpt_en: Mini PCs offer a convenient form factor, but a laptop is ready to go with you anywhere. There's no perfect answer.
excerpt_fa: Mini PCs offer a convenient form factor, but a laptop is ready to go with you anywhere. There's no perfect answer.
content_en:
Mini PC vs. laptop: Which is better for your home office?
A laptop can become a desktop with one cable, making the home-office choice less obvious than it looks.
I own both a mini PC and a laptop, and I prefer to have the mini PC on my desk. It doesn't take up much space and fades into a setup that revolves around the monitor, keyboard and mouse I actually use. The small box becomes a part of the office and an organized desk.
However, a laptop can do the same. Plug one into a big screen via HDMI, throw in a wireless keyboard and mouse, and the basic experience is pretty close. This can get even better with a compatible USB-C or Thunderbolt dock to manage displays, peripherals, networking and charging all in one. When both computers are set up at a desk, the gap between them becomes tiny.
What you're paying for and whether the computer needs to leave that desk are the more important questions.
Mini PCs are often closer to laptops than desktops
While their name implies a desktop PC that's been hit with a shrink ray, there are plenty of mini PCs based on hardware that would be perfectly normal in a laptop. For instance, the ASUS NUC 15 Pro supports Intel's Core Ultra 7 265H (a mobile processor), along with SO-DIMM memory and M.2 SSD storage.
There's a practical explanation for that. When you're attempting to fit a whole computer into a box that's small enough to fit behind a monitor, laptop components are quite convenient. But similar parts don't guarantee identical performance. Cooling, firmware and manufacturer-set power limits all have an impact on what a processor can sustain, especially when you put it to work for more than a quick benchmark. Thus, two machines with the same CPU name can still behave differently.
Upgradeability varies too, which is one of the main downsides of a mini PC. The NUC 15 Pro offers two SO-DIMM slots and two M.2 storage slots on supported configurations, offering greater flexibility for memory and storage upgrades than some thin laptops with soldered memory. Not all configurations include memory or storage from ASUS, however.
That last detail is important for fair price comparisons. When you start adding RAM, an SSD and perhaps an operating system to the list of items, a bargain-looking barebones mini PC can turn into less of a value.
The same reality check applies to graphics. Integrated graphics are just fine for email, office apps, video calls and browser-intensive tasks. If you're doing demanding video editing, 3D work or any other GPU-intensive task, don't assume that the small desktop box has more graphics power than a laptop.
A docked laptop makes this a much tougher choice
A mini PC has straightforward appeal compared to a laptop: you're buying the computer without the built-in screen, battery, keyboard and trackpad that may go unused for the majority of its lifespan. That's largely why I enjoy mine. I prefer to have a machine that's part of the workspace and always available. But a laptop has a pretty good response to that argument, and it's a single cable.
With a compatible docking station, a laptop can connect to external displays, Ethernet, a keyboard, mouse and other USB devices simultaneously. Supported models can also be powered from the same dock (specific capabilities vary by laptop and dock). Close the lid, tuck the machine into a stand and your day-to-day setup can feel like one built around a mini PC.
The difference is evident when you have to travel. Unplug the laptop and the same computer comes with you, including your local files, apps, browser sessions and settings. There's only one machine to maintain — no need to wonder which computer has the document you definitely saved five minutes before a meeting.
But that doesn't mean a laptop is the obvious home-office option. Mini PCs can be compact, flexible and even more cost-effective if your computer doesn't move around much and you already have a monitor and peripherals. If you're a frequent traveler, work in various locations or want to keep everything on one machine, a docked laptop might be the better choice.

title_en: How to add and customize your CarPlay widgets
title_fa: How to add and customize your CarPlay widgets
excerpt_en: CarPlay's widgets let you check info quickly, which is a great option for apps that aren't otherwise supported.
excerpt_fa: CarPlay's widgets let you check info quickly, which is a great option for apps that aren't otherwise supported.
content_en:
How to add and customize your CarPlay widgets
Personalizing your CarPlay dashboard beyond its apps only takes a few easy steps.
Since Apple added widgets to CarPlay in iOS 26, compatible cars have gotten even closer to being a proper extension of your iPhone. Instead of being limited to navigation, messaging and audio, CarPlay widgets let you view information from many other apps on your phone. Whether you want to check live game scores, manage your smart home or follow the forecast at your destination, a widget makes it simple to do so on the road.
Before diving in, you should know there's a difference between a CarPlay app and a widget. An app like Maps or Spotify is fully optimized for CarPlay and takes up most, if not all, of your display for easier interaction. On the other hand, widgets appear in customizable stacks and provide specific details from the app they represent.
Luckily, customizing your CarPlay experience, including widgets, is straightforward. And even better, iOS 27 expanded the available widget pool beyond what was possible before.
How to start adding widgets to CarPlay
While you're parked or not driving, open the Settings app on your iPhone, then go to General > CarPlay and tap your car. Next, select Widgets. Make sure Show Widgets is enabled, then select Add Widget to browse your options.
You'll see recommended choices at the top, followed by a list of compatible apps on your phone. A given app can offer multiple widgets, so make sure to explore them all. The number of widgets that show at a time changes based on the size of your car's infotainment center.
Removing or rearranging widgets is simple. From the same page, use the handles on the right side to drag items and adjust your layout, or hit the red minus button to remove anything you don't want anymore. Some widgets will show a blue i icon to customize them, such as picking one of your saved locations in the Weather app.
At the bottom of the Settings page, you can also toggle some automation options. Turning on Smart Rotate will change to the most relevant widget in a stack based on factors like the time or your location, while Widget Suggestions will display potentially useful ones even if you haven't manually added them.
To access your widgets while on the road, swipe from left to right and you'll find them on the leftmost page. Swipe up or down on a stack to move through them as needed.
Recommended widgets for CarPlay
Widgets can fill gaps that CarPlay apps aren't able to, so there are lots of ways to put them to use. If you ever feel homesick on long trips, add the Photos widget and select any album to show. Meanwhile, if you take full advantage of Apple HomeKit and are worried that you may have left a lamp on, you can turn it off using a Home widget.
Additional first-party options include Reminders, Weather, Clock and Podcasts. An analog clock looks fancy when you don't need navigation, while Weather can tell you when the sun will set or rise. Apple Sports is also an option for following your favorite teams as you drive.
Many third-party widgets offer unique additions to your dashboard, especially after iOS 27's expansion. You can see what your friends are up to using Instagram stories or add the Amazon widget to check your order status and make sure you're home in time. If you're in need of an AI voice assistant in the car, you can utilize widgets for chatbots like Claude and Gemini.
Some widgets are certainly more useful than others; you likely don't need to check your Duolingo streak or see LinkedIn updates while driving. For best results, stick to widgets that provide easily glanceable, non-distracting info.

title_en: Are extended warranties on TVs and laptops ever really worth it?
title_fa: Are extended warranties on TVs and laptops ever really worth it?
excerpt_en: TV and laptop repairs can get expensive in a hurry, so getting a warranty sounds smart. But is it really?
excerpt_fa: TV and laptop repairs can get expensive in a hurry, so getting a warranty sounds smart. But is it really?
content_en:
Are extended warranties on TVs and laptops ever really worth it?
Or are they just another useless upsell?
Have mercy on retail clerks. To keep their jobs, they're often asked to push promotions they know most customers don't want, such as memberships and credit cards. Upselling looks good on a manager's ledger, even if it irritates a good portion of their customers.
If you've been shopping for smart TVs, laptops or just about any major piece of electronics in the past decade, you've no doubt been pitched on the idea of an extended warranty, AppleCare+ and Best Buy Protection being a couple of familiar examples. At a glance, they're more reasonable than most in-store promotions. Everything breaks eventually, and the cost of some repairs can be eye-watering. Just ask anyone who's smashed the display on their MacBook.
Despite this, you can safely skip an extended warranty in most circumstances. They mostly exist for the sake of an upsell, which you can tell by the strings attached and the fundamental nature of consumer electronics. When an extended plan is justified, you'll likely know before you walk in the door.
Why extended warranties are usually a waste of money
For starters, extended warranties are typically focused around defects, and any TV, laptop or similarly expensive device is likely to be covered by the manufacturer for 90 days to a year or more. This matters because if a product is defective, it's going to fail under relatively normal strain, by definition. You're liable to find out quickly if it's faulty, though there are obviously outliers.
Another point is that while planned obsolescence is real, a product that survives the first year is likely to survive past the two- or three-year window that's common for many extended warranties. In an accelerated longevity test by RTINGS, 102 TVs were run nonstop between November 2022 and September 2025. Only two actually failed before they reached 3,000 hours, and most made it to at least 8,000. This longevity test employed TVs that had already been used for hundreds of hours, so the results didn't show an initial spike for models that failed right away — a spike that would be present if the TVs were all brand-new. But again, those failures often are covered by the manufacturer and wouldn't require an extended warranty. If you watched TV for four hours a day, every day, it would take you over two years to reach that 3,000-hour mark, by which point just 2 percent of the TVs had failed.
Unbiased reliability figures are harder to come by for laptops, but it almost doesn't matter for a couple of reasons. The first is that planned obsolescence factor. Within two or three years, just about any device you buy — especially a laptop — is going to be supplanted by something with improved performance for a similar price. Meanwhile, equivalent products are going to become cheaper and cheaper, especially if you're willing to buy a used or refurbished model.
That factors into the second point, which is the cost of an extended warranty vs. just saving up for a replacement or repair. To cover a $1,300 TV, for example, Best Buy charges approximately $160 for two years of Geek Squad TV Protection, and $280 for five years. While the cost of replacing the display panel could vastly exceed either sum, the retailer estimates that other repairs will typically fall between $255 and $395. You could spend most or all of the cost of a repair on a warranty you may never use, and you'll still be stuck with old hardware if you successfully pursue a claim.
Some warranties include loopholes, on that note. We can't make blanket statements, but it's important to watch out for clauses that prevent you from seeking repairs if there are signs of liquid exposure or anything else that could be branded user error, regardless of whether it's the source of your problems. In other situations, you may be forced to use a manufacturer's warranty first if it's still in effect, Geek Squad Protection being a prime example.
When does an extended warranty actually make sense?
Though TVs are rarely mission-critical, there are professionals who simply can't afford any downtime with a laptop or other productivity tools, and put the equipment they own through the wringer. The cost of an extended warranty is nothing by comparison, though if you're in this camp, it's essential that you pick a plan that allows for loaner units or rapid repairs or replacements. In fact, you may be looking at special business-oriented warranties that aren't pitched over the checkout counter.
If you hate the idea of downtime but you're not necessarily a professional, it can make sense to invest in a plan like AppleCare+. That incorporates theft and loss replacements for some devices and vastly reduced prices for fixing accidental damage, including liquids. Considering that many cities have an Apple Store or at least an authorized service site, same-day repairs and replacements are a real possibility.
Unfortunately, most vendors don't have such an extensive support network. If you need a repair, there's a strong chance your device is going to be shipped to a depot in another city, then back a few days later. And they may ship it back unrepaired if they can't replicate the issue you reported — something we've experienced directly. Every warranty is a gamble, in that respect.

title_en: Lucid Motors’ EV output falls to lowest level in almost 2 years
title_fa: Lucid Motors’ EV output falls to lowest level in almost 2 years
excerpt_en: The company is deliberately limiting production after years of struggling to find mass-market demand for its EVs.
excerpt_fa: The company is deliberately limiting production after years of struggling to find mass-market demand for its EVs.
content_en:
Lucid Motors built 2,954 electric vehicles (EVs) in the third quarter of this year, a 54% drop from a year ago, as the company purposely limits production to better meet demand for its EVs.
This was the third straight quarter in which the number of EVs Lucid built has declined. It’s also the lowest quarterly output since the first quarter of 2025, which was just after Lucid Motors started production of its second EV, the Gravity SUV.
Lucid delivered 3,806 EVs in the third quarter, roughly flat with the second quarter and down about 200 vehicles from the third quarter of 2025. The company has struggled to find buyers for either of its first two luxury EVs. In five of the last six quarters, it built more vehicles than it delivered.
Lucid’s new CEO, Silvio Napoli, has spent the last few months leading an effort to “simplify the company.” That effort has included laying off around 1,500 employees, streamlining the company’s leadership, and eliminating a second shift at its factory in Arizona in a bid to reach cost savings of $1.4 billion. Lucid also delayed the release of its third EV, the Cosmos. That model is supposed to be much cheaper, starting at under $50,000.
The third-quarter figures, released Monday afternoon, come just a few days after rival EV upstart Rivian posted its best quarter in history on the back of the R2, its new, more affordable SUV. Although Rivian didn’t break out specific delivery figures for the R2, the company shipped nearly 20,000 vehicles in the third quarter, the first full quarter with the R2 in production, up from 12,194 in the second quarter.
Lucid’s failure to find a large market of buyers for its EVs is even more stark when compared with the promises the company made when it went public in 2021. That year, Lucid Motors merged with a special purpose acquisition company and estimated it would ship as many as 90,000 EVs in 2024 alone. The company raised $4 billion in the transaction.
On Lucid’s second-quarter earnings call in August, Napoli spoke about why he thinks the company has failed to make a dent in the EV market.
“While there is no question that Lucid brought leading innovations and outstanding products to the market, we have disappointed on several fronts, and for far too long,” he said. “We have not executed consistently. We missed commitments, launched products before they were ready, underinvested in service, responded too slowly to quality issues, and allowed complexity to slow decisions down.”
The Cosmos’ lower price could, in theory, let Lucid access a wider market, but Napoli cautioned shareholders that rushing the new EV out could create more trouble.
“We will not repeat the mistakes of the past by bringing a product to market before it is ready,” Napoli said on the call.

title_en: Reverse-engineered games: All the news on video game decomps, recomps, VR and web and 3D ports
title_fa: Reverse-engineered games: All the news on video game decomps, recomps, VR and web and 3D ports
excerpt_en: It’s a wild time for retro gaming. Thanks to decompilations and recompilations of classic titles, those games are becoming unshackled from their proprietary code and original hardware to be ported to new devices or updated in ways to completely change the original game. Ever...
excerpt_fa: It’s a wild time for retro gaming. Thanks to decompilations and recompilations of classic titles, those games are becoming unshackled from their proprietary code and original hardware to be ported to new devices or updated in ways to completely change the original game. Ever...
content_en:
It’s a wild time for retro gaming. Thanks to decompilations and recompilations of classic titles, those games are becoming unshackled from their proprietary code and original hardware to be ported to new devices or updated in ways to completely change the original game. Ever imagined skateboarding in Call of Duty? Or playing the original Halo right in your web browser, complete with multiplayer?
Reverse-engineered games: All the news on video game decomps, recomps, VR and web and 3D ports
These are unofficial versions of games, so they may sit in a legal gray area. It seems unlikely that Nintendo, for example, is particularly happy about people finding ways to play The Legend of Zelda on non-Nintendo hardware. Many of these projects are also made with the assistance of AI, which, for some people, is a non-starter given ethical or environmental concerns surrounding the technology.
Below, you’ll find our coverage of gaming decomps, recomps, and all the other ways gamers are reverse-engineering games to go previously unimaginable places.
- Here’s a video of Half-Life: Alyx running natively on a Vision Pro.
Take a look. It was “made possible” thanks in part to Valve’s ARM port of the game it made for the Steam Frame and with some help from Claude.
- Just think: You could be playing Halo in a web browser right now.
The video game decompilation movement has done it again. Not only do we have 128 player Halo across Windows, Linux, and Android , you can also just fire it up in a web browser thanks to OpenHaloCE and immediately start campaign or a huge multiplayer match. It’s not just one dev: lots of people made this happen.
- This unofficial Lego Racers remake runs in your browser with split-screen and online multiplayer.
The classic game decompilation movement has produced yet another amazing feat: 1999’s Lego Racers isn’t just back, the excellent Mario-Kart-meets-Lego game is anywhere you want it to be. NavigatorSharp’s fan recreation Step On It works in a web browser on desktop or phone, and you can find builds for Android, Mac, Windows PC and Linux (including the Steam Deck) right here too.
How an online community took back the Legend of Zelda
I don’t have a first memory of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time because It’s been in my life for as long as I can remember. Before I had the coordination to play the game myself, I would watch my older brothers play it for hours on end. When I could finally play through it myself, it felt like flying.
I chase that dopamine hit once every year or two by playing through Ocarina of Time, which normally requires dusting off my old GameCube and hoping the disk isn’t too scratched to read. But for the last several months, I haven’t been playing Ocarina of Time on a Nintendo console at all. Instead, I’ve been playing it on something called Ship of Harkinian: an unofficial port of Ocarina of Time for PC that a few short years ago would have been unimaginable.

How an online community took back the Legend of Zelda
I don’t have a first memory of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time because It’s been in my life for as long as I can remember. Before I had the coordination to play the game myself, I would watch my older brothers play it for hours on end. When I could finally play through it myself, it felt like flying.
I chase that dopamine hit once every year or two by playing through Ocarina of Time, which normally requires dusting off my old GameCube and hoping the disk isn’t too scratched to read. But for the last several months, I haven’t been playing Ocarina of Time on a Nintendo console at all. Instead, I’ve been playing it on something called Ship of Harkinian: an unofficial port of Ocarina of Time for PC that a few short years ago would have been unimaginable.

title_en: The Matic is the first robovac to get an FCC ban waiver, not that it needs it
title_fa: The Matic is the first robovac to get an FCC ban waiver, not that it needs it
excerpt_en: The Matic is our favorite robot vacuum and robo-mop, and it's also now the first to escape the FCC's Roomba ban. Well, sort of - because the Matic wasn't banned to begin with. Here's what's actually happening: On October 2nd, the FCC added the original Matic, model 4MA0001, and...
excerpt_fa: The Matic is our favorite robot vacuum and robo-mop, and it's also now the first to escape the FCC's Roomba ban. Well, sort of - because the Matic wasn't banned to begin with. Here's what's actually happening: On October 2nd, the FCC added the original Matic, model 4MA0001, and...
content_en:
The Matic is our favorite robot vacuum and robo-mop, and it’s also now the first to escape the FCC’s Roomba ban.
The Matic is the first robovac to get an FCC ban waiver, not that it needs it
Unlike the router companies, Matic is publicly committing to US manufacturing.
Unlike the router companies, Matic is publicly committing to US manufacturing.
Well, sort of — because the Matic wasn’t banned to begin with.
Here’s what’s actually happening: On October 2nd, the FCC added the original Matic, model 4MA0001, and its charging dock model 4DK0008 to its ban waiver list. That allows the FCC to approve these radio products for import, marketing, and sale.
But the Matic doesn’t need a waiver, because its radios were already approved years ago. The FCC’s foreign drone, robot, and router bans only keep future products from getting imported into the United States, not existing ones whose radios have already been approved.
Besides, Matic’s products don’t get FCC approval to begin with — instead, Matic ships them with an off-the-shelf Intel AX210 Wi-Fi and Bluetooth chip that gets its own approval from the FCC. (It’s the same kind of Wi-Fi card you’ll find inside a desktop or laptop computer.) Matic also doesn’t need to worry about an import ban specifically, because Matic assembles its robots right here in Mountain View, California.
A waiver could theoretically help if Matic were to build new products outside the United States and try to import them here, except that the FCC hasn’t granted Matic a blanket approval on a brand of robot, like it did with Asus and Netgear’s routers. Instead, it specifically granted a waiver for the Matic models 4MA0001 and 4DK0008, which, again, have already made it through the FCC.
The waiver might not be completely symbolic. The FCC is currently trying to close lots of the loopholes that currently make its ban impotent, is weighing whether to make manufacturers disclose all the components in their gadgets, and is retroactively cracking down on some companies it sees as flaunting the rules. While Matic assembles its robots in the US, it admits it doesn’t yet source 65 percent of its components from US suppliers, the threshold for it to be seen as Made in the US, and perhaps one of those foreign components could trip it up if not for the waiver.
Even so, Matic already gets its “core compute platform” from Nvidia, co-founder and president Mehul Nariyawala tells The Verge, and sources other “critical components” from US companies “whenever possible.”
And unlike some of the other companies where the FCC has mysteriously granted a waiver, Matic is committing to more US manufacturing and onshoring.
“Up till 3 months ago, both our R&D offices and production facilities were in the same office in Mountain View, about 24,000 square feet,” Nariyawala tells The Verge. “We’ve turned that entire facility into production facility and moved our office to Menlo Park.”
He says Matic went from shipping 1,500 robots a year ago to 17,000 now, and is trying to find more and more US suppliers so it can use even fewer foreign parts.
“At the moment we might be the only floor cleaning robot built in America,” he says. “That is becoming one of the key value propositions for our product.”
Correction: Nariyawala is Matic’s co-founder and president, not CEO.

title_en: OpenAI will start watermarking ChatGPT’s text in the EU
title_fa: OpenAI will start watermarking ChatGPT’s text in the EU
excerpt_en: OpenAI will watermark ChatGPT and Codex text in the EU to comply with the AI Act. Editing can make the invisible marks harder to detect, it says.
excerpt_fa: OpenAI will watermark ChatGPT and Codex text in the EU to comply with the AI Act. Editing can make the invisible marks harder to detect, it says.
content_en:
OpenAI will start adding an invisible watermark to text generated by ChatGPT and Codex in the European Union to comply with the EU AI Act, the company said Monday in a blog post.
The EU AI Act’s transparency rules, which took effect on August 2, require AI companies to mark AI-generated content in a way other systems can identify.
OpenAI said the watermark will roll out over the coming weeks to eligible ChatGPT and Codex users on all plans, but only in the EU. Developers using OpenAI’s API anywhere in the world can turn it on for select models starting today; it’s off by default. OpenAI said it is not making text watermarking a global default at launch.
The watermark is not an actual symbol, but works by subtly shaping the model’s word choices, leaving a pattern readers can’t see, but a detector can pick up. Because it lives in the words themselves, it travels with the text when it’s copied and pasted. OpenAI said the watermark doesn’t identify the user, and that it saw no meaningful change in its models’ performance with it switched on.
OpenAI also published a technical report for its method, called textGrain, alongside the announcement. Co-written with researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Yale, it walks through an example of using a secret key to sort next-word predictions to finish the sentence. Add hundreds of these nudges together, and the detector can spot AI-generated content using only the text and the key.
Can the watermark be removed by editing? OpenAI’s tests suggest yes. In one test, replacing 10% of words with synonyms dropped detection from about 92% to 66%. The company also said short passages, math answers, and translated text are harder to detect.
“These limitations contribute to our decision to provide initial detector access only to approved researchers and expert organizations, who can help us evaluate reliability and responsible uses,” said the company.
OpenAI also cautioned that a missing watermark “does not prove human authorship.” The text could be too short or too heavily edited, or it could come from another company’s AI.
“[Watermarks] can indicate that an OpenAI system generated or processed part of a passage, but not how much human judgment, editing, or creativity went into it,” the company said.
The announcement comes two months after Anthropic said it would watermark text generated by Claude, a move it’s applying worldwide. That decision drew backlash from some Claude users, who argued they had supplied “the instructions, context, decisions” while Claude was just “the tool.”
OpenAI had built a text watermark before but held off on releasing it, partly over concerns that users would switch to rivals that didn’t watermark, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024.
Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and OpenAI are among the companies that have committed to following the EU’s code of practice on AI-generated content.

title_en: Etched fields funding offers at $40B+ valuation, sources say
title_fa: Etched fields funding offers at $40B+ valuation, sources say
excerpt_en: Just a couple of months after its last big raise, the AI chip startup is already being plied with investment offers at double or more its current value, sources tell TechCrunch.
excerpt_fa: Just a couple of months after its last big raise, the AI chip startup is already being plied with investment offers at double or more its current value, sources tell TechCrunch.
content_en:
Although it’s only been a couple of months since Etched raised $700 million at a $21 billion valuation, the AI chip startup is already being plied with investment offers at double or more its value, according to people familiar with the company.
Etched is reviewing incoming bids that range from $40 billion from top-tier investors to $50 billion from lesser-known backers, one person said. These fundraising talks are early, so terms of any deal, should one happen, may change. Etched declined to comment.
While this may seem like a fast timetable to raise another mega round, Etched is pursuing a particularly expensive segment of the AI industry: building full AI hardware systems powered by its own proprietary chips. The person familiar with these offers said that if it raises as much as its last round, this could give Etched a cushion of as much as 3.5 years of runway.
There are reasons why VCs are hot to own a piece of Etched. The four-year-old startup shows promise of challenging Nvidia. Not only did quant trading firm Jane Street lead the last $700 million round, it is also a customer that took delivery of an early system. Etched said in July that it had already secured $1 billion in customer orders, including the one from Jane Street, after manufacturing its test chip at a TSMC factory this summer.
Co-founder and COO Robert Wachen previously told TechCrunch that investors are so enthusiastic because Etched has designed two new components from scratch to speed up inference — the computing process that happens after a user submits a prompt.
The company claims its chips can process more tokens faster and at a lower cost than Nvidia’s. That’s the reason its processors have been so attractive to Jane Street, for whom a microscopic advantage in speed can yield massive profits.
The startup has also impressed investors with its ability to attract engineers from Nvidia, with roughly 15% of Etched’s 400-person workforce having previously worked at the chip giant, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Etched also operates a new 10-megawatt data center in Silicon Valley and established a facility in Taiwan to coordinate production near TSMC.
Co-founders Gavin Uberti and Chris Zhu famously met in an advanced math course at Harvard, while Wachen was Uberti’s roommate and they dropped out to pursue the company.
In terms of fast rounds at big leaps in valuations, Etched already has a history of them. The startup announced a $300 million round at a $10.3 billion valuation led by Sequoia in July. It announced the $700 million round at a $21 billion valuation in September. Back-to-back funding rounds, which essentially act as a single financing split into two tranches with separate valuations, are increasingly common among the buzziest startups.

title_en: This startup is issuing AI-generated acne prescriptions
title_fa: This startup is issuing AI-generated acne prescriptions
excerpt_en: People in Utah can now use AI to get a prescription for acne treatment. On Monday, healthcare startup Nolla Health announced that users in the state can scan their faces using its app, allowing its AI system to analyze acne severity and autonomously write a prescription, as...
excerpt_fa: People in Utah can now use AI to get a prescription for acne treatment. On Monday, healthcare startup Nolla Health announced that users in the state can scan their faces using its app, allowing its AI system to analyze acne severity and autonomously write a prescription, as...
content_en:
People in Utah can now use AI to get a prescription for acne treatment. On Monday, healthcare startup Nolla Health announced that users in the state can scan their faces using its app, allowing its AI system to analyze acne severity and autonomously write a prescription, as reported earlier by Bloomberg.
This startup is issuing AI-generated acne prescriptions
Utah has signed off on letting Nolla Health’s AI system scan a user’s face and issue a prescription directly.
Utah has signed off on letting Nolla Health’s AI system scan a user’s face and issue a prescription directly.
The service is launching as a pilot program with gradually loosening physician oversight. Two physicians will approve each AI-generated prescription before they’re issued for the first 100 patients, but will start reviewing them only after they’re prescribed for up to 500 patients. “After that, physicians review a sample of at least 10% of prescriptions every month, plus every case involving an escalation or side effect,” Nolla Health says.
Several other healthcare companies are experimenting with AI-generated prescriptions in Utah, which started allowing AI systems to renew certain medications earlier this year. But Nolla Health says it’s the first in the country to issue initial prescriptions, rather than renewals. “The pilot is designed to complement, not replace, physicians,” Nolla Health writes in its press release. “By handling routine, low-acuity cases, Nolla Derm frees dermatologists to focus on complex, high-risk patients.”
The program will cost $4.99 / month, and only applies to Utah residents who are 18 years of age or older and have mild-to-moderate acne. Nolla Health says it will direct users to a physician if its AI system cannot “confidently select a treatment.” The startup’s AI can currently prescribe eight different skin treatments, according to Bloomberg.

title_en: Instagram is toying with a read-only mode for Plus subscribers
title_fa: Instagram is toying with a read-only mode for Plus subscribers
excerpt_en: That's a nicer name than 'stalker mode.'
excerpt_fa: That's a nicer name than 'stalker mode.'
content_en:
Instagram is toying with a read-only mode for Plus subscribers
That’s a nicer name than ‘stalker mode.’
Instagram is internally developing a possible new feature that seems tailor-made to allow for nefarious behavior. Leaker and reverse engineer Alessando Paluzzi posted on X with the discovery of an Instagram feature billed as "read-only mode." According to the uncovered screenshots, this option allows for a session where "you can't like, comment, message, follow or view stories" on the social network, which would allow a user to browse the platform without leaving any type of paper trail about what they were viewing. It appears to be a concept for Instagram Plus accounts from the images shared.
A spokesperson from Instagram told Engadget that read-only mode "is an internal only exploration, not testing externally at all." So this feature is far from launching if it ever does, and tech platforms will regularly try out features that never see the light of day for users. But it also doesn't suggest whether there's any acknowledgement internally that this type of reduced visibility could be used for stalking or other criminal purposes. Hopefully the team can sufficiently address those safety concerns before any potential external tests or launch.

title_en: Wikimedia links OpenAI agents to an outage and unauthorized activity
title_fa: Wikimedia links OpenAI agents to an outage and unauthorized activity
excerpt_en: Wikimedia says it's "deeply concerned about the impact of 'rogue' AI agents on platforms like ours.
excerpt_fa: Wikimedia says it's "deeply concerned about the impact of 'rogue' AI agents on platforms like ours.
content_en:
Wikimedia links OpenAI agents to an outage and unauthorized activity
The foundation says it's "deeply concerned about the impact of 'rogue' AI agents on platforms like ours.
OpenAI agents have been running amok online, and it seems the Wikimedia Foundation has been affected too. The foundation says it detected unauthorized activity from OpenAI agents on its platforms, including edits to some wikis and failed attempts to compromise a note-taking tool. It reiterated that bots have been crawling data from its platforms en masse, while agents that appear to be operated by OpenAI have made millions of requests to its public APIs.
An investigation didn't turn up any evidence that AI agents were using Wikimedia systems to coordinate their activity (as they appear to have done on non-Wikimedia-operated wikis) and nor did the foundation detect signs of its data or systems being compromised. "However, we are concerned about what could have occurred here, the difficulty and effort involved in investigating and attributing this activity, and the growing risks of agentic AI activity on our platforms in general," Selena Deckelmann, the foundation's chief product and technology officer, wrote in a blog post. "The open web is a public good. We should not allow this behavior to become the 'new normal' for the people or organizations that maintain it." Engadget has contacted OpenAI for comment.
It appears OpenAI agents edited some Wikimedia wikis without permission. Almost all of these were test edits in sandbox sections of wikis and weren't visible on pages that users would generally access. There were also "a few edits to the configuration for a citation tool, which we believe were potentially malicious edits that were intended to misuse this tool as a proxy for fetching data from remote services," Deckelmann wrote. While bots are permitted to edit Wikipedia under certain conditions, approval was not sought in these cases. (The English version of Wikipedia prohibits AI-generated articles.)
Moreover, agents that Wikimedia believes to stem from OpenAI attempted to compromise a note-taking tool called Etherpad, but those efforts failed. "Agents unsuccessfully tried to use it to fetch data from other websites as a proxy," Deckelmann wrote. "Other agents also likely operated by OpenAI took notes about their tasks, though this did not appear to turn into coordination."
The Wikimedia Foundation previously said that bots have been hammering its platforms since early 2024 to scrape data for generative AI training purposes. It now says agents have crawled millions of pages — mainly from Wikidata and Wikimedia Commons — and made "hundreds of thousands of data queries" to the Wikidata Query Service, which may have helped cause an outage in May.
"AI companies are not doing enough to secure their systems and protect the public from the harm they cause," Deckelmann argued, adding that Wikimedia is "deeply concerned" about the effect rogue AI agents can have on open knowledge platforms such as the ones it operates.
"Bots and agents are part of the future of the web, and the companies who unleash and profit from them must directly help avoid and repair damage they can do," Deckelmann wrote. "Our collective priority should be the health of the overall web ecosystem so that it continues to benefit all people — not just a handful of billionaires."
Wikimedia has offered a dataset for AI training purposes in an attempt to dissuade crawlers from scraping its platforms, which increases its costs and can potentially overload its systems. The foundation has also partnered with several tech companies to offer them streamlined access to data, but OpenAI isn't among them.

The Wikimedia Foundation previously said that bots have been hammering its platforms since early 2024 to scrape data for generative AI training purposes. It now says agents have crawled millions of pages — mainly from Wikidata and Wikimedia Commons — and made "hundreds of thousands of data queries" to the Wikidata Query Service, which may have helped cause an outage in May.
"AI companies are not doing enough to secure their systems and protect the public from the harm they cause," Deckelmann argued, adding that Wikimedia is "deeply concerned" about the effect rogue AI agents can have on open knowledge platforms such as the ones it operates.
"Bots and agents are part of the future of the web, and the companies who unleash and profit from them must directly help avoid and repair damage they can do," Deckelmann wrote. "Our collective priority should be the health of the overall web ecosystem so that it continues to benefit all people — not just a handful of billionaires."
Wikimedia has offered a dataset for AI training purposes in an attempt to dissuade crawlers from scraping its platforms, which increases its costs and can potentially overload its systems. The foundation has also partnered with several tech companies to offer them streamlined access to data, but OpenAI isn't among them.

title_en: After Factory’s public spat with Khosla, Menlo proudly invests
title_fa: After Factory’s public spat with Khosla, Menlo proudly invests
excerpt_en: Days after Vinod Khosla called Factory a struggling also-ran, Menlo has shown up with a check and a glowing blog post.
excerpt_fa: Days after Vinod Khosla called Factory a struggling also-ran, Menlo has shown up with a check and a glowing blog post.
content_en:
Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy and his team announced Monday in a blog post that the firm has invested in AI coding startup Factory.
Menlo declined to comment on how much it invested but said the deal was part of Factory’s latest funding round announced last month at a $5 billion valuation. A source familiar with the deal told us the investment was significant to Menlo — not a token gesture — and that Menlo would have invested more had there been room on the cap table.
Ordinarily, something like this wouldn’t necessarily be news; startups often extend previous rounds to add new investors. But last week, Factory co-founder and CEO Matan Grinberg was embroiled in a very public airing of dirty laundry when he alleged that he had fired investor Chris Degnan of firm RPT Partners from his role as board advisor. Grinberg said he feared Degnan may have shared confidential information with Factory’s biggest competitor, Cognition. The accusation followed Degnan’s move to Cognition as its chief revenue officer.
A who’s who of the tech industry came out of the woodwork either to support Degnan and condemn Factory, or vice versa, but none was more surprising than Vinod Khosla. Khosla’s firm is an investor in both Factory and Cognition. But that didn’t stop the venerable VC from calling Factory a desperate “struggling second tier competitor,” and accusing Grinberg of lying about firing Degnan and impugning his character. Degnan disputed Grinberg’s story, saying he resigned and that he’d rebuffed a competing job offer from Grinberg.
So Menlo’s full-throated endorsement of Factory, which praised its founders, its tech, and its relationship with its customers, is more than a feather in Factory’s cap. It’s a statement that Factory is not in the state that Khosla implied it was.
Murphy famously bet his firm on Anthropic back when it appeared to be an also-ran to OpenAI and has been on a hot streak ever since, landing deals with Lovable and Legora, for instance. So now some VCs are calling Factory “the next Anthropic.“
Sequoia’s Shaun Maguire, also a Factory backer who came out on X in support of Grinberg last week, appears thrilled with Menlo’s endorsement, saying the firm is “on a tear.” Notably, Menlo is not an investor in competitor Cognition.

title_en: Reflection debuts Beam, an open-weight AI model to rival Chinese models at lower compute cost
title_fa: Reflection debuts Beam, an open-weight AI model to rival Chinese models at lower compute cost
excerpt_en: Reflection is aiming Beam and future models at enterprises and sovereign nations. The pitch is to build “AI factories,” a product that would let institutions build their own customized, local AI system by training Reflection’s AI models on their own proprietary data.
excerpt_fa: Reflection is aiming Beam and future models at enterprises and sovereign nations. The pitch is to build “AI factories,” a product that would let institutions build their own customized, local AI system by training Reflection’s AI models on their own proprietary data.
content_en:
Reflection AI is officially unveiling Beam, its first frontier, open-weight AI model. The two-year-old, Brooklyn-based startup claims Beam matches the performance of leading Chinese open models on advanced reasoning benchmarks at dramatically lower costs, a claim that could heat up the race to build a Western answer to DeepSeek, Qwen, and Z.ai.
Reflection’s announcement confirms reporting from Axios over the weekend that the startup was close to a launch. The company shared new details in a lengthy blog post Monday, which described Beam as a text-only mixture-of-experts model trained on high-compute reinforcement learning to be effective at reasoning, coding, and agentic tasks at “a fraction of the token cost and inference time compute” of rivals.
Beam is a 501-billion-parameter model with 23 billion active parameters. It was pretrained on 23.8 trillion tokens and has a 1 million token context window. To compare, Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 has roughly 744 billion total parameters with 40 billion active.
Reflection’s performance claims haven’t been independently verified, but on advanced reasoning benchmarks, the company says Beam scores on par with Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 and outperforms today’s leading Western open models while using “3-4x less inference compute.” Reflection calls it a “workhorse model” for enterprises, the public sector, and developers.
Reflection is positioning itself against closed labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, against popular open models from Chinese developers, and against Western players like Mistral, Meta, and Cohere. Its most direct U.S. rival might be Inkling, the open model from Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Lab released in July. Reflection’s own benchmarks show that Beam outscores Inkling on four coding tests where both report results, but Inkling is a multimodal model and Beam is text-only.
Reflection was founded in 2024 by two former Google DeepMind researchers and has raised roughly $4.7 billion from backers, including Nvidia, Sequoia Capital, and Lightspeed Venture Partners, per PitchBook. Its last round valued the company at a $25 billion pre-money valuation.
The startup has also been locking up compute — a key ingredient needed to train frontier models capable of luring customers away from Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s closed models, as well as the cheaper open-weight models from Chinese labs. This summer, Reflection signed deals collectively worth more than $7 billion with SpaceX and Nebius to secure access to Nvidia’s GB300 chips through 2029.
Reflection is aiming Beam and future models at enterprises and sovereign nations. The pitch is to build “AI factories,” a product that would let institutions build their own customized, local AI system by training Reflection’s AI models on their own proprietary data. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company backs Reflection, has long championed the “AI factory” idea and pushed to strengthen the open AI ecosystem — a vision that would also benefit Nvidia, whose GPUs would power those systems.
Axios reported that hedge funds and trading firms are among those eager to build such systems. Reflection has already begun testing the concept of a sovereign AI factory partnership with Shinsegae Group in South Korea.
Reflection says it will release Beam’s weights and full technical details this month, with distribution through hyperscalers and neoclouds and integrations across open source libraries at launch.
Reflection did not respond in time to TechCrunch’s requests for more information.

title_en: All the drama around AI’s takeover of mathematics
title_fa: All the drama around AI’s takeover of mathematics
excerpt_en: This past year, OpenAI, Anthropic, and other labs have announced breakthroughs on numerous long-standing mathematical problems, in some cases pushing well beyond what researchers expected current systems to be capable of — including resolving one of the famous Millennium Prize...
excerpt_fa: This past year, OpenAI, Anthropic, and other labs have announced breakthroughs on numerous long-standing mathematical problems, in some cases pushing well beyond what researchers expected current systems to be capable of — including resolving one of the famous Millennium Prize...
content_en:
This past year, OpenAI, Anthropic, and other labs have announced breakthroughs on numerous long-standing mathematical problems, in some cases pushing well beyond what researchers expected current systems to be capable of — including resolving one of the famous Millennium Prize problems. But in classic Silicon Valley style, AI labs are moving fast and breaking things, barreling through the discipline with all the grace of a runaway bulldozer. Results that might normally have been celebrated have instead sparked backlash. AI labs say they are learning from earlier mistakes. Whether those promises bear fruit remains to be seen.
Read on below for the latest updates in the AI takeover of mathematics.
OpenAI keeps bulldozing mathematicians
In a chaotic few months, OpenAI has demonstrated it can do two things with remarkable consistency: make impressive breakthroughs in mathematics, then colossally screw up announcing them. OpenAI is now trying to do better. Somehow, it has botched that too.
OpenAI’s latest attempt to repair fractured relations with a mathematical community it has repeatedly alienated is to consult a new independent advisory group of elite practitioners. But mathematicians speaking to The Verge, including one of the group’s members, describe a messy and confusing affair bearing many of the hallmarks of OpenAI’s previous rushed forays into mathematics, suggesting the company has learned little from its mistakes. And then there’s the daunting task the group has been handed first: helping coordinate the release of scores more results OpenAI says its unreleased model has produced, the prospect of which is already stirring dread among researchers over what this looming tidal wave of breakthroughs could do to their field.
Read Article >OpenAI wants to consult elite mathematicians about how to not fumble again
After turning a string of spectacular mathematical results into a reputational crisis, OpenAI is consulting human mathematicians to help it figure out a less disastrous path forward.
On Monday, the company announced a new independent panel of mathematicians tasked with advising it and other AI companies on their interactions with mathematical research and the wider mathematics community, including how new results are presented and released. Its abrupt arrival caught many mathematicians by surprise. Researchers told The Verge the group is a good first step, but many said they were left with basic questions about what it will actually do, how much influence it will have, and whether OpenAI will actually listen to it, as well as concerns over whether such a small group of prominent researchers can represent the wider mathematical community.
Read Article >OpenAI just wants to win
OpenAI has spent the last few years planting flags across the increasingly difficult terrain in mathematics. This week, it claimed one of its biggest prizes yet: a solution to a legendary Millennium Prize problem. In normal circumstances, this would have been celebrated as a historic achievement.
Instead, many mathematicians have watched OpenAI’s relentless advance with growing unease. To them, the company appears less like an enthusiastic newcomer than an impossibly well-resourced interloper, charging into problems they have dedicated their lives to studying with little apparent regard for long-standing norms or the consequences for those left in its wake. At the heart of that unease is a sense that OpenAI is doing mathematics for different reasons. Mathematicians want to advance the field. OpenAI wants to win.
Read Article >Mathematicians want proof OpenAI didn’t use their work
Another researcher is challenging OpenAI about the data driving its increasingly impressive array of mathematical discoveries. Just days after a bitter row erupted over whether the company’s models benefited from unpublished work, a second mathematician has come forward accusing the AI giant of unethical and “dishonest” behavior and a lack of transparency about the origins of its training data.
In a series of posts on Mastodon, mathematician Andreas Thom raised concerns that interactions he and his colleagues had had with the ChatGPT chatbot before OpenAI’s triumphant announcement may have contributed to its success in the field. One of the 10 results OpenAI announced with great fanfare last month involved Thom’s area of expertise, so-called non-sofic groups, and OpenAI acknowledged that their result built heavily on previous work by Thom and fellow mathematician Gábor Kun.
Read Article >OpenAI’s sly mathematical breakthrough sends a chill through academia
OpenAI’s announcement Tuesday that it has solved one of mathematics’ legendary Millennium Prize problems should have been a moment of triumph. The result is both an undeniable achievement and a striking demonstration of just how rapidly AI is transforming mathematics. But before it was even formally announced, the breakthrough had been complicated by the unusual circumstances that prompted OpenAI to pursue the problem: After hearing other researchers were making progress, it seems to have thrown its considerable resources into a last-minute effort to beat them to the punch. The ensuing controversy has surfaced allegations of scooping, spying, and flagrant violations of long-standing academic norms that researchers fear could have a chilling effect on the field.
As Abhishek Saha, a mathematics professor at Queen Mary University of London, explains it, OpenAI has engaged in the “kind of things that mathematicians will generally not do.”

title_en: Arc Raiders and The Finals are both getting TV and film adaptations
title_fa: Arc Raiders and The Finals are both getting TV and film adaptations
excerpt_en: There aren't many details on these upcoming game adaptations just yet.
excerpt_fa: There aren't many details on these upcoming game adaptations just yet.
content_en:
Arc Raiders and The Finals are both getting TV and film adaptations
We don't have too many details just yet.
The era of video game adaptations continues. Chernin Entertainment just inked a deal to adapt both Arc Raiders and The Finals as TV and film projects, according to a report by Variety. Embark Studios, who published both games, will also be involved in some capacity.
We don't have any actual details here, other than some corporate press releases that boast about "the next big step in growing" both franchises and how this will offer "integrated transmedia experiences." The president of Chernin did say that these are "ambitious global IPs with the potential to become major franchises across film and television." It sounds like the company is proposing a couple of shared cinematic universes, but that's conjecture on my part.
These titles aren't exactly known for their narrative experiences. Arc Raiders is a fun third-person extraction shooter and The Finals is a free-to-play FPS set inside of a game show. This means that the filmmakers can pretty much do whatever they want, so long as the world-building remains intact.
Chernin does have a nice pedigree for this type of thing, especially in recent years. It helped produce Backrooms for theaters and The Madness for Netflix. Past releases include The Last House, Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes and the Fear Street trilogy, among many others.
This is just the latest adaptation of a video game. Helldivers is getting a movie next year, followed by Elden Ring and Call of Duty in 2028. We also aren't too far from that long-anticipated The Legend of Zelda film.

title_en: Wikipedia operator says OpenAI’s ‘rogue’ bots may be linked to a May outage
title_fa: Wikipedia operator says OpenAI’s ‘rogue’ bots may be linked to a May outage
excerpt_en: Following many recent disclosures about AI agents accessing third-party websites and services, the Wikimedia Foundation, which hosts Wikipedia, says that it "can confirm that we have discovered some activity" by "rogue" OpenAI agents on Wikimedia platforms. The activity includes...
excerpt_fa: Following many recent disclosures about AI agents accessing third-party websites and services, the Wikimedia Foundation, which hosts Wikipedia, says that it "can confirm that we have discovered some activity" by "rogue" OpenAI agents on Wikimedia platforms. The activity includes...
content_en:
Following many recent disclosures about AI agents accessing third-party websites and services, the Wikimedia Foundation, which hosts Wikipedia, says that it “can confirm that we have discovered some activity” by “rogue” OpenAI agents on Wikimedia platforms.
Wikipedia operator says OpenAI’s ‘rogue’ bots may be linked to a May outage
The Wikimedia Foundation believes OpenAI agents edited wikis, tried to ‘exploit’ a notetaking tool, and made ‘millions’ of automated API requests.
The Wikimedia Foundation believes OpenAI agents edited wikis, tried to ‘exploit’ a notetaking tool, and made ‘millions’ of automated API requests.
The activity includes edits to Wikimedia wikis, “unsuccessful attempts” to “exploit” the Etherpad note-taking tool that the Wikimedia Foundation hosts, and heavy traffic that the foundation says “may” have contributed to a partial outage that happened in May, according to a blog post. However, the Wikimedia Foundation says it didn’t find evidence that its systems were “used for coordination among agents” (recently, OpenAI bots reportedly hijacked a German wiki site to coordinate) or evidence of systems or data being compromised.
Here’s Wikimedia’s summary of what it saw:
Wiki editing: We’ve identified edits to Wikimedia wikis that we believe are from AI agents operated by OpenAI. These edits were not published to pages with visibility to general readers; almost all of them were testing edits in “sandbox” areas of the wiki. It also included a few edits to the configuration for a citation tool, which we believe were potentially malicious edits that were intended to misuse this tool as a proxy for fetching data from remote services. While Wikipedia policies allow bots to edit when they are disclosed and approved by the community, none of those approvals were sought in these incidents.
Etherpad probing and use: Agents we believe to be operated by OpenAI made some unsuccessful attempts to compromise our public Etherpad, a note-taking tool we host as a community service. Agents unsuccessfully tried to use it to fetch data from other websites as a proxy. Other agents also likely operated by OpenAI took notes about their tasks, though this did not appear to turn into coordination.
Excessive data downloading: Agents we believe to be operated by OpenAI made millions of automated requests to our public APIs to access the knowledge on Wikimedia projects, crawled millions of pages (mainly from our projects Wikidata and Wikimedia Commons), and made hundreds of thousands of data queries to the Wikidata Query Service (WQDS). This traffic may have contributed to a partial outage on WQDS in May.
“The open web is a public good,” the Wikimedia Foundation says. “We should not allow this behavior to become the ‘new normal’ for the people or organizations that maintain it.”
“We appreciate the detailed findings Wikimedia shared with us,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in a statement. “We’re working with them as we review and analyze the activity they identified along with our overall investigation, and we’ll continue to share relevant information as that work progresses.” OpenAI’s investigation hasn’t been able to verify if its bots contributed to the May outage, according to Pusateri.
Update, October 5th: Added statement from OpenAI.
