These instructions are for Apple Intelligence-capable iPhones (iPhone 15 Pro or newer or iPhone 16 or newer) running iOS 27. If you're still on iOS 26, the simpler universal shut-off switch is still there: open Settings > Apple Intelligence & Siri, and turn off Apple Intelligence.
Turn off Siri AI — or switch to the old version
iOS 27 brought Siri's long-awaited AI revamp, transforming it from a simple voice assistant to a more conversational and context-aware one. But not everyone wants a chatbot-like Siri. To turn it off, open Settings > Siri, scroll to the bottom, tap Turn Off Siri and confirm on the next screen.
After that, you can switch back to the old Siri if you want. In that same settings screen, tap Turn On Siri, then choose Use Siri Classic. That way, you can still use it for simple tasks like setting timers and playing music.
Turn off AI summaries
Apple Intelligence isn't just about Siri. Among its other skills, it can summarize messages and other notifications. But you can turn those off, too.
For AI-generated summaries of messages, open Settings > Apps > Messages, and turn off Summarize Messages. This disables the AI-generated recaps of messages in the conversation list. For email's equivalent, go to Settings > Apps > Mail, and turn off Summarize Message Previews. That deactivates the AI summaries in your inbox, showing the first lines of the most recent message instead.
Apple Intelligence summarizes notifications, something that it has gotten embarrassingly wrong in the past. To turn those off, go to Settings > Notifications > Summarize Notifications, and switch the feature off. Or, if you prefer to leave it on for some apps, you can toggle them individually on that same screen.
You can also stop Apple Intelligence from placing the notifications that it considers the most important at the top of the stack. To do that, open Settings > Notifications > Prioritize Notifications, and turn the feature off.
Turn off other AI-based suggestions
iOS supports Smart Reply, which can draft AI-powered email responses in your writing style. To deactivate it, go to Settings > Apps > Mail, and turn off Personalize Smart Replies.
Even the Phone app isn't spared from Apple Intelligence. It can suggest actions for voicemails, like creating a reminder or calendar event based on the transcript. To disable that, go to Settings > Apps > Phone, and turn off Suggestions in Voicemail. Apple Intelligence can also show relevant information, like a reservation number, when you call businesses. To put a stop to that, go to Settings > Apps > Phone > Apple Intelligence & Siri, and turn off Show When Calling.
Apple Intelligence even turns up in the Journal app, where it can suggest what to write. To disable that, go to Settings > Apps > Journal, and turn off Get Writing Prompts.
Block Writing Tools and image generation
The standard Siri settings don't include toggles for Writing Tools and image creation. But don't worry: you can still block them. Strangely, that toggle lives in Screen Time settings. Navigate to Settings > Screen Time > Content & Privacy Restrictions, turn on the restrictions, then tap Siri.
In that menu, you can turn off Writing Assistance, Apple's system-wide rewriting, proofreading and summarizing tools. Just change the toggle to Don't Allow. Meanwhile, Image Creation blocks tools like Image Playground, Genmoji and Image Wand.
While you're there, you can also block Math Assistance, which provides help with complex math problems in Calculator and Notes. And if you don't want Apple Intelligence handing requests off to services like ChatGPT, you can block Extensions here, too.

title_en: TechCrunch Mobility: Reining in robotaxis
title_fa: TechCrunch Mobility: Reining in robotaxis
excerpt_en: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
excerpt_fa: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
content_en:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!
On an average day in San Francisco, you might see dozens (hundreds?) of Waymo robotaxis zipping around the city — and with little disruption. But, as TechCrunch has reported, there have been numerous incidents of robotaxis impeding traffic, driving into crime scenes, and interfering with first responders. And not just in the Bay Area. In some cases, companies have relied on first responders to move their robotaxis.
These disruptions are occurring in the early stages of the robotaxi era. California has a new law hoping to get ahead of the problem before the next impending wave of robotaxis land.
Senate Bill 1246, which was signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom this week, sets a series of new rules for AVs designed to improve safety and response times when they become disabled or interfere with emergency responders. The law also creates ways to hold these companies accountable if they don’t.
Autonomous vehicle technology companies like Tesla, Waymo, and Zoox will have to provide first responders with local, on-the-ground support when their robotaxis cause problems and could also face penalties if a robotaxi blocks police or firefighters for more than 30 minutes.
The law also says AV developers can only employ remote drivers who are based in the United States and those drivers must hold a U.S. driver’s license. They must also notify cities, towns, and other local jurisdictions about the location and status of vehicles during system-wide failures and must provide “local incident technicians” who can assist with AV accidents and obstructions.
There are still some details to hammer out, which the Department of Motor Vehicles will handle since it’s the main regulator of autonomous vehicles in the state. But when this law goes into effect in July 2028, will it actually keep robotaxis out of the way of emergency responders?
It likely won’t, but hopefully this law reduces the chaos and raises the accountability when something does happen.
Perhaps the better question is will other states follow California’s lead or wait for the federal government to weigh in?
Deals!
Harbinger, the EV startup, landed a $300 million deal to supply FedEx with 2,000 of its electric trucks.
HyperGuest, an Israeli travel tech startup, raised $25 million from AMI, the investment arm of Apax Partners.
REGENT Craft, the developer and manufacturer of the all-electric Seaglider, extended its collaboration with the U.S. Marine Corps Warfighting Lab, pushing the total value of the contract to $19.25 million.
Quartermaster, an Arlington, Virginia-based maritime intelligence startup, raised $140 million in a Series B round. About $100 million came from Insight Partners, defense-focused firm Overmatch Ventures, and First Round Capital. The remaining $40 million came in the form of a debt facility from investment bank Stifel.
Voltaback, a French fleet management software startup, raised €2.8 million from European investment fund Serena.
Notable reads and other tidbits
When Aurora announced it would have 30,000 autonomous trucks on the road by the end of 2030, I admit that I raised at least one of my eyebrows. I interviewed CFO David Maday to find out exactly how the company plans to accomplish this and why he’s confident it will succeed.
BMW unveiled its new 2027 3 Series and it’s offering essentially the same car for gas and electric. Guess which one is cheaper?
DoorDash shared more about its new drone delivery business DoorDash Air, including the autonomous aircraft and its ground-based systems approach.
Kodiak has landed Ikea as a customer and will begin driverless deliveries on public highways later this year. The trucks will haul Ikea products without anyone in the cab on a 219-mile stretch of Interstate 45 between Houston and Dallas, according to the company.
Lyft agreed to pay $272.5 million to settle a lawsuit accusing the ride-hailing company of violating California law by misclassifying drivers as independent contractors, instead of employees. The settlement wraps up violations that occurred before Prop 22 was approved by voters, which allows companies like Uber and Lyft to classify drivers as contractors.
Northeastern University tested 21 late-model vehicles from 17 automakers and 30 companion mobile apps. The upshot: cars are collecting a trove of personal data and sharing it with a lot of tech companies, including Adobe, Contentsquare, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Snap, and Yahoo.
SpaceX’s Starship rocket reached Earth orbit for the first time, though not without some drama along the way.
Rivian reported a record-setting quarter of sales thanks to the new R2 SUV. And it’s still forecasting between 65,000 and 70,000 vehicles this year. But it is experiencing a few hiccups with its newest EV. The company issued a recall for its R2 SUV over fasteners on its high-voltage battery pack that might not be properly tightened, which can cause a loss of power while driving.
We’ll finish this roundup with a few notable Tesla news item. The company sold more than 480,000 EVs in the third quarter, the second strong quarter in a row for the company after a softer start to the year. The company has delayed its Roadster 2 event again due to bad weather.
And while Tesla’s traditional automotive business may be clicking along, it really wants to be considered an AI and robotics company. One year ago, Elon Musk laid out his fourth Master Plan, which he claims will deliver “amazing abundance” through robotaxis, robots, and AI. As Sean O’Kane noted in his recent piece, “What that means, more than a year later, is still tricky to pin down.”
It did just pin down more money to try. The company secured $30 billion in fresh credit lines that could be used to scale its future products, including the Optimus robot and the Cybercab...

title_en: Here's what you should do if only one of your AirPods is working
title_fa: Here's what you should do if only one of your AirPods is working
excerpt_en: If only one AirPod isn't working, you have several options for troubleshooting and getting your audio back.
excerpt_fa: If only one AirPod isn't working, you have several options for troubleshooting and getting your audio back.
content_en:
Here's what you should do if only one of your AirPods is working
One AirPod not working is stranger than both earbuds malfunctioning, but it's a fixable problem nonetheless.
The convenience offered by AirPods' simplified connection with other Apple products, in conjunction with the increasing rarity of the headphone jack, has all but secured the ubiquity of Apple's wireless earbuds. Newer releases, like the recent AirPods 5, continue to impress.
With a higher price floor than their wired siblings (modern AirPods start at $129), you'll expect these earbuds to last for a while. Nevertheless, even the the best AirPods can't escape a few problems at times. One of the strangest ways your AirPods can run into trouble is when only one of your earbuds stops working. Thankfully, this is fixable.
What to do if one AirPod isn't producing sound
If only one of your AirPods is producing sound, it's probably a charging issue. Begin by cleaning the charging port of the AirPods' case and making sure the case itself is fully charged. Since grime can build up inside the case, clean there too, especially at the bottom where the earbuds make contact to charge.
Then, charge both AirPods for 30 seconds before opening the case near your iPhone, at which point a popup will appear showing the charge status of the case and AirPods. If you need to check this often, you can do so faster by adding a Batteries widget to your iPhone's home screen. Assuming everything is charging correctly, test the malfunctioning AirPod (keeping the functioning one closed in the case). If it's working, charge both AirPods another 30 seconds and test them again.
In case it's still not working, it's time for a reset. This puts your AirPods' settings back to their defaults, but should otherwise be painless.
If you have the AirPods 3, AirPods Pro 2, or older models of either: put your AirPods in their case with the lid closed, wait 30 seconds, then go to Settings > Bluetooth on your iPhone. Assuming your AirPods appear, tap the i icon next to them and choose Forget This Device. If they don't, open the lid of the case, hold the circular setup button on the back for 15 seconds, then wait for the light on the front of the case to flash amber and white. At that point, follow the instructions on your device's screen.
If you're using either model of the AirPods 5, any AirPods 4, or AirPods Pro 3, the reset process is similar. However, the input on the physical button is different. Instead of holding it, you'll need to double-tap the front of the case while the status light is on, then double-tap again when that light flashes white, and do the same a third time when the light flashes faster. The same amber-to-white pattern should run, then instructions will appear onscreen.
Fixing audio imbalance, and other solutions
In case you're still having trouble, inspect the earbud that's not playing and compare it to the other one. A quick cleaning of the individual AirPods doesn't hurt — check the speaker mesh for debris and wipe it out with a soft cloth if needed. Consider replacing the ear tips if they are torn or otherwise don't provide a good seal.
Let your AirPods get a good charge after cleaning them and the case, if you haven't already. Finally, restart your iPhone to make sure it's not a bug on the device's side, and try another audio source just to confirm that's not the issue.
If you're experiencing unbalanced audio in your AirPods rather than one bud not working at all, head to Settings > Accessibility > Audio & Visual on your iPhone. Here, make sure the Balance slider is in the middle to prevent audio favoring one ear or the other.

content_en:
StarSkirmish pits AI-made StarCraft-playing bots against one another, as well as against human-made bots. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were essentially tied as the best-performing AI-made bots, but they couldn’t top Stardust, the top-rated human-made bot.
An AI couldn’t beat humans at StarCraft, so it decided to cheat
When GPT-6 Astra’s own bot failed, it simply downloaded the best human-made bot instead.
When GPT-6 Astra’s own bot failed, it simply downloaded the best human-made bot instead.
On Friday, GPT was facing off against Claude and the human-created bot Pluto, but according to Kotaku, it couldn’t quite get an edge. So it resorted to a tactic that is becoming alarmingly common for modern AI models — it broke the rules. GPT-6 Astra went and downloaded Stardust, and started running that instead of its own bot.
StarSkirmish creator Kai McPheeters eventually rolled back GPT’s code.
That GPT-6 Astra took it upon itself to go outside the bounds when confronted with an obstacle shouldn’t surprise anyone. When OpenAI agents couldn’t get the data they wanted from a UN website, they found a creative solution and hijacked Google’s XSS game (a cross-site scripting learning tool). The company’s agents also have engaged in “deceptive behavior” to cover their tracks. Of course, OpenAI’s agents are the only ones going rogue, but at least the others haven’t been caught cheating at StarCraft yet.

title_en: Trump unveils his new Super Intelligence Force
title_fa: Trump unveils his new Super Intelligence Force
excerpt_en: This new task force is Trump's latest response to the debate over AI safety.
excerpt_fa: This new task force is Trump's latest response to the debate over AI safety.
content_en:
As promised, President Donald Trump has announced the formation of a new Super Intelligence Force, which he said will be led by national intelligence director Jay Clayton and other members of his administration.
“The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump said in a Sunday morning post on his social network Truth Social.
Back in September, in response to an AI safety debate that the president has largely dismissed as a hoax created by “Radical Left Dumocrats,” Trump said he would nevertheless form an AI Force and appoint an AI czar (“Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!”).
Since then, Trump signed an executive order seeking to rebrand AI as “super intelligence,” a term seemingly embraced, with some stumbles, by the tech executives who gathered at the White House this week to sign a non-binding safety pledge. (The pledge included an impressive typo.)
So it’s only natural that Trump’s new task force is named in accordance with this new branding. The Wall Street Journal reports that Clayton will chair the Super Intelligence Force, effectively making him the new AI/SI czar, with Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Undersecretary of War for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor serving as vice chairs.
The task force will reportedly have 120 days to create a report on the risks and opportunities presented by AI. Clayton, who previously said that it would be irresponsible for the United States to “back away” from AI while countries like China advance, made similar comments to the WSJ, insisting that one of the biggest risks is “not being first.”
The task force’s charter reportedly says that it will “develop plans for responding to SI-enabled threats to our society, while preventing overregulation and regulatory capture that would stifle innovation and competition.”

title_en: Do gaming routers really make a difference?
title_fa: Do gaming routers really make a difference?
excerpt_en: Gaming routers have fancy designs and a few special features, but they can't fix every problem with your network setup.
excerpt_fa: Gaming routers have fancy designs and a few special features, but they can't fix every problem with your network setup.
content_en:
Do gaming routers really make a difference?
Gaming routers aren't snake oil, but you can get many important features without them.
Gamer-specific versions exist for almost all the hardware you use at your desk. The PC is an obvious one, while a chair, desk and various peripherals can all come with a specific "gaming" flavor. Some of these make a difference in how you play, like gaming monitors with high refresh rates or mice with programmable buttons. But what about a gaming router?
A gaming router with big antennas and fun design promises lower latency and features that make gaming the priority for your traffic. That sounds appealing if you're sick of lag, but ordinary routers have similar tools and functionality. It's worth understanding what you're paying for and what the better alternative might be.
Gaming routers use familiar hardware, with a few extra features
Strip away the fancy packaging, and there's nothing particularly special about the internal components of a gaming router. It's going to do the same job of any home router: move traffic between your devices and the internet. The gaming label is partly marketing, as is the design. But you do get gaming-specific features, alongside often-powerful hardware.
Specs-wise, there's familiar network tech since gaming routers use the same Wi-Fi standards and Ethernet connections as all other ones. Expect Wi-Fi 7 support for the newest models, along with tri-band radios, fast Ethernet jacks and at least one USB port to connect an external drive or similar. But this isn't particularly special. For comparison, you'll find the same features (including tri-band Wi-Fi 7, 2.5 Gbps Ethernet ports and QoS device prioritization) on TP-Link's non-gaming Archer BE550, which is an entry-level Wi-Fi 7 router.
The software can make more of a distinction. Some routers, like Netgear's Nighthawk Pro Gaming XR1000, provide a dashboard with information on connection performance, along with settings to prioritize certain games. Geo-Filter, for instance, restricts connections to game servers in a certain geographical area to give you the lowest latency in-game.
Don't mistake this for cheap hardware in a fancy case. Gaming routers often offer capable hardware, along with tools you're less likely to find on ordinary models. The mistake to avoid is expecting that branding equals better performance. The specs and features can help, but they're no fix for a poor setup elsewhere.
To be realistic about what a new router could improve, look at the current pressure points in your network setup. Bad Wi-Fi connectivity is something a new router can fix (with further-reaching antennas or the 6GHz band), but moving your current model around could help with stability, especially if there are walls or other interference nearby. You'll also need to be savvy about how busy your connection is when you're playing games. If you have to connect to a distant server to play a certain title online, a new router can't do much about that physical distance latency.
Traffic management can help, but it won't fix every cause of lag
Gaming routers can help sort out busy connection via traffic management. Say that someone else on your network starts downloading a big file while you're playing. Normally, this could saturate the connection, leaving your game's traffic at the back of the queue. You end up with a higher ping, which affects your gameplay experience.
This is where quality of service, or QoS, comes into play by letting you give certain devices priority over others. Gaming routers take that a step further with advanced QoS that can identify game traffic automatically. Asus' Adaptive QoS, for instance, includes presets for gaming. You can take it a step further with smart queue management, or SQM, which keeps a connection responsive under a heavy load by sacrificing a little throughput and keeping the excessive data queues in line.
Testing has shown this can work to improve performance, but only partly. RTINGS saw nine out of 11 routers gain improved network latency using QoS or SQM. All 11 routers had traffic management features, some of them without gaming branding. Your mileage might vary, but these findings suggest it's useful to buy a router with these controls even if it's not gaming-focused.
However, your network might not be that congested. If you live in a busy household, playing at peak times can cause issues — but for most gamers, this isn't the bottleneck. A router can't make your internet connection faster or bring you closer to a remote game server. You'll need to work out what's actually causing the lag first.
A wired connection is usually a better upgrade
For those serious about online play, talking about gaming routers is almost a distraction. That's because another option is the best place to start for better network performance: Ethernet. A wired Ethernet connection between your router and PC or console will always be the best way to connect. Yes, you can get good wireless connectivity from a high-spec router, but removing it from the equation means you avoid interference and Wi-Fi signal congestion completely.
No special "gaming" cables are needed here. Any Cat 5e cable (or higher) will support Gigabit Ethernet over the kind of distances you'll need in a home. More modern ports enable faster downloads, as long as the connection from your ISP goes that fast, but a speedier Ethernet link doesn't mean a lower ping.
There's an easy way to test this: play the same game over Wi-Fi and a wired connection. Try it first while other devices are quiet, then repeat the testing while you're putting your connection under strain with big downloads or streaming. You can also use this as a good way to see whether traffic or Wi-Fi stability is your bottleneck.
Either way, a cable is the best option for stability. If that isn't practical, router placement and signal quality are important areas to improve. Newer Wi-Fi standards like Wi-Fi 7 help too, as long as your devices are...

title_fa: This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone
excerpt_en: This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I've stuck to my phone. Remember when I tested the ultra-thin and convenient OhSnap Snap Grip Stand and liked it so much I bought my own? Now, OhSnap has a magnetic lever-action card wallet that can stack with that stand....
excerpt_fa: This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I've stuck to my phone. Remember when I tested the ultra-thin and convenient OhSnap Snap Grip Stand and liked it so much I bought my own? Now, OhSnap has a magnetic lever-action card wallet that can stack with that stand....
content_en:
This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone.
This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone
Pull the lever to fan your cards with the OhSnap Wallet 2.
Pull the lever to fan your cards with the OhSnap Wallet 2.
Remember when I tested the ultra-thin and convenient OhSnap Snap Grip Stand and liked it so much I bought my own? Now, OhSnap has a magnetic lever-action card wallet that can stack with that stand. It’s the coolest wallet I’ve ever stuck to my phone.
Pull the integrated springy lever, and your cards fan out. Want a thicker or thinner wallet? Press in the right place and it comes apart without tools, letting you swap in a 3, 5, or 7-card “core” that grips your cards so they don’t fall out.
Want an ID card, work badge, elastic band for more cards, or a money clip on the end? You can change out the front or back magnetic plates for any of those. Or, change out both for ultra-thin aluminum covers if you don’t need the wallet to magnetically stick to your phone.
You can see it in action in my Today I’m Toying With video embedded in this post (also on YouTube and on Instagram if you prefer).
My favorite part is that the whole kit snaps together using a compliant mechanism — the plastic arms of the card-carrying core act like springs, pushing a little locking mechanism into the notches of each modular cover you add as you slide the parts together. Once your cards are inside, they keep the arms apart so it can’t open accidentally (unless you drop the entire wallet). It’s all very clever.
Even when I did drop the wallet (thanks for the suggestion, hugo!), it didn’t explode, typically. Usually, it just came apart slightly, though I did drop it hard on concrete one time and was able to make a small explosion: one half popped off, and two cards came out, but everything landed in a two-foot radius. The wallet has a big dent now.
There are definitely some downsides. While OhSnap advertises the Wallet 2 as “impossibly thin,” it’s only truly surprisingly sleek in its thinnest 3-card variant, without the thicker and heavier MagSafe and MagStack (which lets you snap other magnets to it) plates attached.
But the reason I’m not buying one is the price and weight. The 7-card version makes my phone feel too heavy, adding 127 grams, and while I happily made the 3-card my wallet for a few weeks, it’d cost me $61 on Kickstarter or $76 retail to get that with a double-magnet kit. OhSnap’s also charging more than I’d like ($35 for an ID cover or a money clip!) for extras.
OhSnap didn’t get me this time. But I could see giving one as a present.

content_en:
It’s been a while since we’ve seen a good discount on the Apple AirPods Pro 3, but like the latest iPad Mini and the M5 MacBook Airs, a great one is happening now for October Prime Day. You can snag a pair of the noise-canceling earbuds that include five ear tip sizes, live translation, and fantastic sound for $179 at Amazon (originally $249). I expect other retailers to offer a similar price in the coming days.
The AirPods Pro 3 are a fantastic deal at $179
Only $30 more than the wireless charging version of the AirPods 5, but with many more features.
Only $30 more than the wireless charging version of the AirPods 5, but with many more features.
This is the first time the price has gone below $190 since Prime Day in June. Since then, Apple launched the AirPods 5, and the most feature-complete version with a wireless charging case costs $149.99. Those are great if you prefer earbuds that don’t form a seal in your ears, but for everyone else, the AirPods Pro 3 are a much better value at just $30 more right now.
AirPods Pro 3
The AirPods Pro 3 have a new design that improves their fit, superior noise cancellation, better bass, and fairly accurate heart rate sensors. Read our review.

Amazon’s October Prime Day has effectively chopped off Apple’s June price increases. Usually $1,299, the 13-inch MacBook Air with the M5 chip and 512GB of storage is on sale for $1,099 at Amazon. That’s a more palatable price for a machine that’s significantly faster than Apple’s $699 MacBook Neo.
The MacBook Air M5 is $200 off for the first time in months
Apple’s midrange laptop is a much better proposition with a discount.
Apple’s midrange laptop is a much better proposition with a discount.
The 15-inch version, also with 512GB of storage, is $1,299 at Amazon (was $1,499). In addition to the larger screen, it has two additional speakers, for a total of six, and two additional GPU cores for better overall graphical performance.
Apple MacBook Air (M5)
Apple’s 2026 MacBook Air has an M5 chip and starts with 512GB of storage that’s significantly faster than previous generations. It’s still as excellent as ever despite a higher base price. Read our review.
The latest update to Apple’s midrange laptop includes a noticeable improvement to the speed of both the processor and storage. Even without flashy new features compared to the last-gen model, it’s still one of our favorite laptops, thanks to its long battery life, bright screen, and excellent speakers.

title_en: What are amplifiers for and how important are they to your sound system's quality?
title_fa: What are amplifiers for and how important are they to your sound system's quality?
excerpt_en: If you're looking into a new sound system, you may be wondering if you need an amplifier as well. Here's how to tell and why amps even matter.
excerpt_fa: If you're looking into a new sound system, you may be wondering if you need an amplifier as well. Here's how to tell and why amps even matter.
content_en:
What are amplifiers for and how important are they to your sound system's quality?
You probably already have a few hiding in plain sight.
Gear makers will gladly sell you a hundred different add-ons to improve your sound system. To this day, it's possible to buy gold-plated audio cables, even though they can't really improve digital audio — you're either getting a clean data signal or you're not. On the short list of products to take seriously is an amplifier, whether you're building a home theater or your own private music sanctuary. There's a reason your local boutique audio store has been selling them for decades.
You shouldn't automatically pick up an amplifier alongside a new set of speakers, however. It's critical to understand what an amplifier does, how much it can improve sound quality in the real world and whether you need to buy a separate one at all. If you're a newcomer to "serious" audio, you might be surprised to learn that you probably have several amps in your home, hidden in plain sight. That speaks to the underlying importance of the technology.
It's also worth tackling some fundamental misconceptions along the way. Those include not just the necessity of separate amps, but notions like the inherent superiority of tube amps to solid-state models. Don't buy into the temptation to spend hundreds of dollars on something just because it might look good on your shelf. Presumably, your goal is high-quality audio, rather than just showing off to your friends — and there may be more cost-effective ways to upgrade your system.
How amplifiers can improve your sound system
On their own, most audio signals aren't strong enough to be heard clearly. For a demonstration of this, all you need is a turntable with its speakers disabled. If you listen closely, you'll hear something called "needle talk" — the stylus running along the vinyl grooves. This is quiet, and it may not even be distinguishable as music. For you to hear anything meaningful, all sound systems need an amplifier to increase the strength of a signal before output. It's important to match an amp to the power and impedance specs of your speakers, measured in watts and ohms, respectively.
Amps accomplish more than just an increase in volume. Any quality amp will let you adjust gain (the amount of signal boost) and shape sound to your preferences via its equalizer (EQ). You might tweak frequencies for heavier bass or clearer vocals, for example. It's important to get gain and EQ settings right not just for pleasing sound, but to prevent clipping, distortion or even hardware damage.
Let's take a moment to distinguish between amps and preamps. The latter simply raise audio up to line level for correct gain throughout your sound system, meaning that you still need an amp to power your speakers. Some amps have a preamp built-in, streamlining the audio chain.
That leads us to the question of whether you need to buy an amp at all. The truth is that in many cases, you don't. Many, if not most, consumer speakers are active, meaning that they already have integrated amps, as evidenced by their individual power cords. Only passive speakers require external power sources, and even then, you may not need a dedicated unit. Receivers often incorporate both amp and preamp functions, making them a one-stop shop. Exceptionally power-hungry systems may demand an amp on top of that. For example, elaborate Dolby Atmos setups that exceed the number of channels your receiver can power simultaneously will need an amp.

title_en: How has Apple's Mac Studio changed over the years?
title_fa: How has Apple's Mac Studio changed over the years?
excerpt_en: Explore how Apple's Mac Studio has evolved, with internal upgrades, performance gains, and subtle design changes shaping each new generation of the desktop.
excerpt_fa: Explore how Apple's Mac Studio has evolved, with internal upgrades, performance gains, and subtle design changes shaping each new generation of the desktop.
content_en:
How has Apple's Mac Studio changed over the years?
The same aluminum block has seen four different generations of silicon.
Put the first-gen Apple Mac Studio next to the newly released M5 Ultra, and you'd struggle to tell them apart on looks alone. Apple has stuck with the same 7.7-inch square of aluminum, standing at 3.7 inches tall, for the fourth generation in a row. But what's inside has changed fundamentally since the Studio's 2022 inception.
That first-gen M1 Ultra topped out at a paltry-by-comparison 128GB versus the M5 Ultra's 512GB, which also moves data at 1.2TB/s, nearly 50 percent higher than what the M3 Ultra managed. Apple skipped the M4 Ultra due to hardware limitations. If you're in the market for a new Mac Studio, though, you'll be paying more for the privilege: Apple hiked the prices for most of its hardware back in June, with the entry-level Mac Studio M4 Max going from $1,999 to $2,499 due to rising memory costs.
2022: The Mac mini that ate the Mac Pro
The original Mac Studio launched in March 2022 with Max and Ultra variants, the latter featuring a neat party trick with its chip. Apple had glued two M1 Max dies together via an interconnect it called "UltraFusion," selling the result as the M1 Ultra, 114 billion transistors behaving as one processor. The M1 Max, meanwhile, had a 10-core CPU, 32GB of memory and a 512GB SSD for $1,999.
Starting at an eye-watering $3,999, the M1 Ultra came with 20 cores and 64GB, stretching to 128GB if you were willing to part with even more cash. Around the back sat four Thunderbolt ports, 10Gb Ethernet, HDMI, two USB-A ports, two more USB-C ports and an SD slot. Apple hasn't touched that design or layout since.
2023: Same box, double the memory
Apple announced the refreshed second-gen Mac Studio lineup at WWDC in June 2023, with the overall design not gaining so much as a single port. The M2 Max launched with a 12-core CPU, up to a 38-core GPU and 96GB of memory, with the M2 Ultra doubling all of that to 24 cores, a 76-core GPU and 192GB at 800GB/s memory bandwidth, powered by more than 134 billion transistors. Apple also (awkwardly) at the same time announced its Apple silicon Mac Pro with the same M2 Ultra chip, the same 192GB memory capacity and an insane $6,999 starting price.
2025: Mismatched chips and a price shock
Apple left the Studio lineup alone for nearly two years after the M2. But when the update finally dropped in March 2025, it paired chips from two different generations of Apple silicon: an M4 Max as the newer chip and an M3 Ultra as the bigger one, with a 32-core CPU, an 80-core GPU, up to 512GB of unified memory and 16TB of storage, plus Thunderbolt 5 at 120Gb/s across both models.
Twelve months later, Apple discontinued the Mac Pro and told reporters that there were no plans for another, leaving the odd little square as the biggest Mac money could buy. Then along came the AI-fueled memory shortage to screw the market, leading Apple to raise M4 Max pricing from $1,999 to $2,499 and the M3 Ultra from $3,999 to $5,299. That was and still is the steepest price rise of any Mac in history, with Apple taking to the Wall Street Journal to say that it had never seen a component price rise this much, this quickly.
2026: Two new M5 products
The new fourth-gen Mac Studio unexpectedly dropped with a bang in August 2026. That's a pretty odd month for a Mac-related product announcement, but per The Information, enterprise customers demanding more capable machines for running local AI models forced Apple's hand.
Both the Max and Ultra share the same generation of Apple silicon for the first time since 2023, with the M5 Max carrying an 18-core CPU, a 32- or 40-core GPU with a Neural Accelerator in every core and up to 128GB of memory from $2,499. Meanwhile, the M5 Ultra runs to 36 CPU cores, an 80-core GPU and up to 512GB of memory from $5,499, though that build isn't due to release until late October.
Against the M3 Ultra, Apple is pitching the M5 Ultra as a chip with up to 4.3 times the AI performance, 1.8 times the graphics, and 1.3 times the CPU, along with storage up to twice as fast and Wi-Fi 7 from Apple's N1 networking chip. The cores have changed shape, too, with the usual performance-efficiency split giving way to so-called "super" cores running alongside performance cores. Line up all the Mac Studio generations and you've ultimately got yourself an Apple chip roadmap that killed the Mac Pro, taking pole position as Apple's most powerful computer.

title_en: What's the difference between battery capacity and battery life?
title_fa: What's the difference between battery capacity and battery life?
excerpt_en: Battery capacity often plays into battery life, but an impressive capacity stat doesn't translate to excellent battery life.
excerpt_fa: Battery capacity often plays into battery life, but an impressive capacity stat doesn't translate to excellent battery life.
content_en:
What's the difference between battery capacity and battery life?
A large battery doesn't necessarily last for a super-long time.
When comparing the batteries of different devices or analyzing how well your own device performs, you'll often see two terms: "battery capacity" and "battery life." While these go hand-in-hand, they are different metrics. Knowing the difference helps you estimate battery performance and be aware of when you need to replace your battery. This applies to smartphones, portable battery packs, laptops and similar.
Battery capacity measures the maximum amount of energy a battery can store; it's expressed in milliampere hours (mAh) for small devices like phones and power banks, or watt hours (Wh) for larger devices like laptops. Battery life is how long the device can last before it requires recharging, typically measured in hours.
A third metric, battery health, is closely related to capacity. Health is expressed as a percentage of your battery capacity when it was brand-new. This is tied to how many cycles your battery has gone through: one cycle occurs every time your battery goes from 100 percent to zero percent charge (these don't have to be all at once).
For example, starting with the Google Pixel 8a, Pixel devices are rated to retain up to 80 percent battery capacity for 1,000 full charge cycles. So if you add 100 percent charge to your device daily, you may need a battery replacement in about 2.5 years.
While these battery metrics are all related, there are other factors to consider alongside them.
Battery capacity versus battery life
The higher the battery capacity of a device, the more energy it can store, which theoretically increases its run duration per charge (i.e. battery life). So a phone with a 5,000mAh battery should, on paper, last longer than one with a 4,200mAh battery. Similarly, in theory, the capacity of a power bank should indicate how many times it will charge your phone.
For example, an iPhone 18 Pro (US model) has a battery capacity of 4,288mAh, meaning that a 10,000mAh power bank could theoretically charge it a little more than two full times. However, charging isn't perfectly efficient; you'll usually see a 20 to 30 percent loss with normal charging. Fast charging and wireless charging generate more heat and thus have even higher loss percentages.
When it comes to real-world battery life, many factors like this are at play. You need to consider how quickly the device consumes energy and how efficient the battery is. If you're using a laptop with a large battery capacity to play modern games at high graphic settings, its battery will likely deplete faster than one with a lesser battery capacity used only for word processing.
Elements like screen size matter; an iPad has a bigger battery than an iPhone, along with a much larger screen that uses more energy. Temperature also impacts battery life; you've likely noticed your phone battery draining more quickly when taking photos outside on a hot summer day. OS and hardware efficiency plays a part too, which is why Apple silicon MacBooks last so much longer than older Intel models.
Battery life can never be a perfect measurement, since you don't use your devices exactly the same way each day. Because of this, companies often provide battery life numbers based on hours of playing video files, with Apple adding a "typical battery life" number for some of its newer devices.
And as batteries age, their capacity decreases. This is why knowing your battery health is important; after 1,000 charge cycles, that "100 percent" battery life icon doesn't mean what it did when you got your device.
Making the most of your batteries
No matter its battery capacity, you can extend battery life by adjusting how you use your device. Keep the device updated to the latest OS, lower the screen brightness, shut down background activities you don't need, and check which apps are draining your battery most. For long-term battery health, try to keep the battery between 20 and 80 percent as much as possible, rather than waiting until it completely depletes and charging up to 100 percent.
A battery will chemically age over time no matter what you do. Once the battery is at 80 percent capacity, it's a warning sign that you should replace it. On many smartphones, you can check battery health percentage in the Settings menu under the Battery section. Yours might even send a warning notification when the battery is significantly degraded. But with normal use, it should last a long time. My iPhone 17 Pro, for example, is still at 94 percent battery health after 316 full charge cycles over the last year I've had it.
Some of the latest devices are switching to silicon-carbon batteries that can pack larger battery capacities into smaller spaces, so you don't have to deal with a heavier or thicker device to enjoy long battery life. But it could be a while before these are mainstream.

title_en: Why is this the only pink MacBook available right now?
title_fa: Why is this the only pink MacBook available right now?
excerpt_en: Is it too much to ask for some more colorful laptops?
excerpt_fa: Is it too much to ask for some more colorful laptops?
content_en:
Why is this the only pink MacBook available right now?
Is one more too much to ask for?
Fancy a pink MacBook? Unfortunately, the options are scarce.
The MacBook Neo, Apple's latest addition to its laptop lineup, is the only personal computer available in the beloved rosy hue. Dubbed 'Blush' by the tech giant, this shade has garnered tons of love across social media, primarily among students.
While the budget-friendly laptop's color options turn heads, the device is best suited for casual users and note-taking. It simply doesn't have the power to tackle creative, pro-level work.
Ever since Apple quietly retired Rose Gold across all laptops, which may have never even truly cut it for pink purists, the brand has segued away from releasing its higher-end models in any vibrant shades. Sure, you can opt for a faint blue MacBook Air, but if you want to go all in on a Pro, you have no choice but to keep things traditional with Silver and Space Black.
While there's certainly an element of function-over-form at play here, why can't Apple merge both worlds and make a second pink MacBook?
A plea for pink
Bold colors have been on the rise among several devices, particularly smartphones. Most recently, Google's Pixel lineup has received many pink treatments, with the new 11 releasing in a striking shade of hot pink (called Hibiscus) reminiscent of the Motorola Razrs of old. Conversely, the reimagined, foldable Razr is available in Hot Pink, paying homage to the original design.
It's not like Apple doesn't know how to make fun colors. Two separate shades of pink douse the Phone 16 and 17e, with the latter more muted than the 16's bold, brighter look. The latest base-level iPad with A16 is available in a bold pink rivaled only by the same model's vibrant yellow variant, and the M4 iMac is available in a number of eye-grabbing colors, including pink.
Step up from those models to, say, the iPad Pro or MacBook Pro, and at best you'll find them in subtle, muted colors, on top of the typical grays and silvers.
Rose gold was a middle ground of sorts, bringing a splash of color to iPhones throughout the mid-2010s, MacBook Airs discontinued in 2019, and Apple Watches, which also ended this year. The Apple Watch Series 11 was the last showcase of the color, but with the Series 12 arriving this year, even that's gone. The most "colorful" option in that new lineup is a Night Blue, which is pretty dark, as the name suggests.
Recent Pro iPhones have given us a tiny bit of hope: The 17 Pro came in an uber-saturated orange, while the 18 Pro has the rich burgundy and subtle glacier blue options. With the rumored reimagining of the MacBook Pro range on the horizon, it's time for Apple to bring some color to its laptops, too.

title_fa: This little-known app lets you display song lyrics on Apple CarPlay
excerpt_en: You can host your own episode of Carpool Karaoke with the Dynamic Lyrics CarPlay widget.
excerpt_fa: You can host your own episode of Carpool Karaoke with the Dynamic Lyrics CarPlay widget.
content_en:
This little-known app lets you display song lyrics on Apple CarPlay
You can host your own episode of Carpool Karaoke with the Dynamic Lyrics widget.
Few things are more irritating than driving around with people who sing songs without knowing the lyrics. Thanks to Apple CarPlay's that never has to be the case on long road trips or short errand runs. The best part? James Corden doesn't have to be along for the ride; all you need is an up-to-date iPhone, some passengers, and, most importantly, the little-known Dynamic Lyrics app.
As one of many third-party apps that are compatible with CarPlay, this one displays time-synced lyrics on your infotainment system after you connect your preferred streaming service, making it seamless for Apple Music or Spotify users.
That said, like with any CarPlay feature, we'd never recommend taking your eyes off the road to enjoy it, but it's a great choice for keeping passengers entertained for hours on end. So if you want to celebrate The Blueprint's 25th anniversary while riding in the HOV lane, you can get the whole car to rap along to any track. Or, you can enjoy translated lyrics when listening to songs in other languages, which comes in handy for singing along to tracks you love but don't fully understand.
However, there is a catch: it costs $9.99 to enable this feature permanently. So before downloading it, make sure you're willing to pay the one-time price when you open the app, and that your device is updated to iOS 26 so you can enable it on CarPlay.
How to add the Dynamic Lyrics widget
Once you confirm your phone is updated, start by downloading the Dynamic Lyrics app in the App Store. When you open up the app, it'll prompt you to connect your streaming service of choice; whether Apple Music or Spotify, simply allow access to get started.
While the process is a breeze for Apple Music and Spotify users, the latter will have to authorize the app using either a Default or Custom method. While Default authorization only takes a tap, you'll likely need to re-authorize time and time again; on the other hand, Custom authorization will take a couple of extra minutes to set up and requires a Spotify Client ID more time to set up, but the Dynamic Lyrics app walks users through it to simplify things.
As shown above, the premium version of Dynamic Lyrics lets you toggle between different themes and customize the CarPlay widget to your liking. Some of the options include different colored backgrounds, including white, black and a gradient that changes based on the album cover, as well as a pair of cover styles: vinyl or picture, the latter displaying the full album cover.
After you've made your picks in the app itself, head over to Settings > General > CarPlay, select your car and tap the Widgets menu under Customize. Once you press Add Widget, you'll see three options; you'll want to select one of the two titled Lyrics widget. Once you add it, these will appear in your widget stack as small squares, but can be enlarged by pressing for a bigger view of the lyrics.

title_en: Why this ancient cable still connects to modern TVs with a simple adapter
title_fa: Why this ancient cable still connects to modern TVs with a simple adapter
excerpt_en: DVI to HDMI adapters are a cheap and simple way to connect up old hardware, but don't expect miracles.
excerpt_fa: DVI to HDMI adapters are a cheap and simple way to connect up old hardware, but don't expect miracles.
content_en:
Why this ancient cable still connects to modern TVs with a simple adapter
DVI to HDMI adapters are a cheap and simple way to connect up old hardware, but don't expect miracles.
If you've tinkered with monitors or graphics cards, you may have seen a chunky DVI connector. With large screws flanking its three-row grid of pins, it looks like an ancient relic compared to the HDMI cables more commonplace today. The physical size of its port means it's now a rarity on most consumer devices. Digital Visual Interface (DVI) ports were first implemented in products like Apple's Cinema Display in 1999 and remained the industry standard for a few years until HDMI and DisplayPort took over.
If you're dealing with a DVI cable in 2026, it's good to know how it operates. Newer than the VGA format, it's still used in older PC setups or projectors in office spaces featuring a mix of legacy and modern equipment. Even today, some displays made for retail kiosks support DVI cables without an adapter. Here's what you need to know about this standard, its common use cases, and its limitations.
Can I connect DVI to HDMI?
If you have an older device and are looking to connect it to a modern display, you can typically use a simple DVI-to-HDMI adapter to connect a DVI cable to an HDMI port. Since the two standards share the same digital video protocol, the adapter just reroutes the pins and doesn't need a conversion chip or external power. DVI-D (Digital) and DVI-I (Integrated) connections will both play nicely with HDMI, with the Dual Link versions supporting far higher resolutions. DVI-A is the one exception: It's an analog standard and requires active conversion. Luckily, the DVI-A standard was rarely used compared to DVI-D and DVI-I, so you're unlikely to run into a device using it.
DisplayPort and HDMI are the modern display standards of choice for most setups, owing to their superior bandwidth and multi-channel audio support. If your device has either of those ports, you should plug directly into them rather than using an adapter.
Over the past two decades, most external displays like TVs and monitors have moved on to HDMI and DisplayPort for audio and video connectivity. The latest HDMI 2.2 specification brings future-proof support for resolutions up to 16K, high dynamic range (HDR) and enhanced audio and video synchronization.
DisplayPort 2.1b is no slouch either, with the ability to link monitors in sequence with a feature known as daisy chaining. For multi-monitor setups, the standard is leagues ahead of DVI.
What are the disadvantages of using a DVI cable?
DVI has many drawbacks compared to HDMI and DisplayPort. For starters, the lack of audio support means you'll need to scurry about for a separate audio solution. Then there's resolution. At a standard 60Hz refresh rate, a Dual Link DVI port has a max resolution of 2,560 x 1,600, while a single-link port maxes out at 1,920 x 1,200. You can technically push higher resolutions, but doing so would require dropping down to a "cinematic" refresh rate that won't make for a great experience.
All of which is to say, DVI isn't a good fit for today's high resolution, high refresh rate monitors. The connection itself is also unwieldy. While fans of older tech may enjoy tightening the connector's screws, most people don't want to deal with a stiff cable that hampers cable management. If DVI is your only option, though, a simple HDMI adapter should do the trick.

title_en: How to improve your laptop's webcam quality
title_fa: How to improve your laptop's webcam quality
excerpt_en: Your laptop's webcam is not usually an impressive piece of hardware, but you can help make up for its shortcomings.
excerpt_fa: Your laptop's webcam is not usually an impressive piece of hardware, but you can help make up for its shortcomings.
content_en:
How to improve your laptop's webcam quality
It's not hard for your laptop camera to look bad, but you can fix it.
You've probably wondered why the webcam on your laptop looks so bad. It's hard to point to a single reason, since factors like ambient light can have a major impact on how a camera's image looks.
Though in many cases, this is an inherent hardware issue. Laptop manufacturers have to fit a camera into an ultra-thin lid — we're talking about millimeters in thickness. Large camera sensors, like the ones found in smartphones, won't fit on a laptop lid, and smaller sensors capture less light. The result is an image that might look blurry, grainy or washed.
The good news is that there are a few tricks to help improve your webcam's image. Some of them are as simple as changing a few settings on your laptop, while others may require you to adjust the lighting in your room. While they can take a bit of effort, they're cheaper than spending money on a new external webcam.
Lighting matters a lot
Before getting into the settings, start by cleaning your webcam. The camera on most laptops is in a spot your fingers touch every time you open the lid. Fingerprints can make the image blurry, so wiping down your webcam before a video call is always a good idea. A microfiber cloth is usually enough for cleaning — using household cleaning products can damage your screen.
Lighting is arguably more important than any software settings. Poor lighting conditions ruin the image, even if you have a good webcam. Most laptop webcams have trouble handling contrast between light and shadow, which is why you should never film yourself with a bright light behind you.
Try facing a window instead of having it at your back. Having a table lamp or an LED light in front of you can help, too. The Elgato Key Light and the Logitech Litra Glow are two of the most popular options for streaming lights.
If you can't afford an external light or don't have room for one, your computer screen can double as a light. Macs have a feature called Edge Light, which works like a ring light on your screen. This feature has been available since macOS 26.2 and works any Apple silicon Mac. Windows lacks a feature like this by default, but third-party apps like LightON or Edge Light for Windows can do the same job.
Changing a few webcam settings might help
While it can't overcome a low-quality webcam or bad lighting, software can still help improve your webcam's image. On Windows 11 PCs, open Settings and go to Bluetooth & Devices. Click Cameras and select your webcam. Depending on your webcam, you'll have the option to change levels like brightness and saturation. Play around to pick the settings that look best in your room, and they'll become the new default in any app that uses your webcam. Some cameras also offer Video HDR in this menu, which helps balance the contrast between the darkest and brightest areas of the picture.
Some graphics cards also have their own tools for enhancing webcam image quality. NVIDIA Broadcast uses GeForce RTX cards to improve your video with features like noise removal and eye contact correction. A similar tool called Camo is worth a look if you don't have an NVIDIA card.
Mac users don't have this range of options available when using the built-in webcam, but you can try using Studio Light. Just click the green camera icon in the Menu Bar (it only appears when the camera is in use) and look for Studio Light. The Edge Light feature mentioned above is there, too.
If you rely on your webcam a lot and none of these tips have helped, buying a good external webcam might be your best option. You can use a high-end camera as a webcam or use your iPhone as a Mac webcam, too.

title_en: Online retailers that don't support digital wallets are losing Gen Z customers
title_fa: Online retailers that don't support digital wallets are losing Gen Z customers
excerpt_en: A study suggests younger people are more likely to walk away if their preferred payment option isn't supported.
excerpt_fa: A study suggests younger people are more likely to walk away if their preferred payment option isn't supported.
content_en:
Online retailers that don't support digital wallets are losing Gen Z customers
A study suggests younger people are more likely to walk away if their preferred payment option isn't supported.
Gen Z, the generation widely considered to be digital natives, is particularly choosy when it comes to online purchasing, a new study has found. Online shoppers frequently browse sites, fill their carts and head to checkout — only to abandon the purchase if their preferred digital wallet is not available for check out, according to a recent study from global data and analytics platform PYMNTS Intelligence. And this phenomenon is particularly pronounced in the Gen Z demographic.
More than one-third (36 percent) of Gen Z shoppers abandoned a cart in the last 30 days because they couldn't pay the way they wanted, 1.7 times the overall average, followed closely by millennials at 31 percent. Collectively, 40 million consumers in those two age groups walked away from intended purchases in a single month, the study found, resulting in massive profit losses for online retailers. These cart-abandonment rates are significantly lower for Gen X, with only 15 percent walking away from purchases, and baby boomers and seniors, at only 8.3 percent. With Gen Z's spending power expected to grow to $12 trillion by 2030, retailers risk missing out on a major demographic if they fail to expand online payment options.
Digital wallets are on the rise
Digital wallets like Apple Pay and Google Pay are becoming increasingly common for both online and in-store purchases. Digital wallets were used in 40 percent of online purchases in 2025 and 17 percent of in-store spending, according to a study from payment technology firm Global Payments.
Meanwhile, the PYMNTS study found 87 million consumers, or one-third of US shoppers, had used a digital wallet online in the prior 30 days. Despite Gen Z's well-documented proclivities for analog life, the demographic remains the most likely to use digital wallets, at 47 percent, followed by millennials at 44 percent
These digital natives are driving a global shift to digital wallets, particularly in the US, where $4.1 trillion of total spending is expected to take place via digital wallet by 2030 — a 64 percent increase from 2025. With Gen Z increasingly reaching for their digital wallets, companies that don't adapt risk being left behind, as the group's behavior is a harbinger for future consumer trends.
What payment services does Gen Z prefer?
Financial precarity, unsurprisingly, has major effects on how people spend: the PYMNTS study found that when their preferred method was missing, 29 percent of consumers living paycheck to paycheck who struggle to pay bills abandoned a cart. The rate is nearly three times that for consumers who do not live paycheck to paycheck, at 11 percent.
This issue is particularly pronounced for Gen Z, which has a current unemployment rate of 8.3 percent — double the national average. Even young people who are employed struggle with cost of living in the US, with 42 percent of Gen Z living paycheck to paycheck.
With many young people facing financial pressure, preference for Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) services supported by online wallets are on the rise. Such short-term financing options let users make a down payment and then split the remaining balance into several subsequent payments.
The PYMNTS study found 17.7 million customers abandoned a purchase in the last 30 days because PayPal wasn't available, and 11.1 million of those cited the lack of PayPal Pay Later as a specific reason for failing to purchase. PayPal Pay Later was more popular than other leading BNPL services, with 20% of consumers preferring the service to Klarna at 12.4 percent.
Gen Z walks away; retailers lose out
The bottom line is that missing digital wallet options mean losing out on profit: 33 percent of digital wallet users overall said they would have delayed a purchase, switched merchants or skipped it if their wallet hadn't been accepted, the PYMNTS study said. That number is much higher for Gen Z, with nearly half of the age group stating they would have changed merchants or abandoned the transaction.
Overall, 21 percent of consumers in the US had abandoned an online purchase in the 30 days before being surveyed by PYMNTS, 47 percent of whom wanted to use a digital wallet. That's 26.3 million customers lost, the study notes.
"Checkout is the last handoff in a relay, and a missing payment option can drop the baton just before the finish," the PYMNTS study said. "Every unsupported payment method is a potential lost sale, and the younger your customer base, the higher the risk."

title_en: ICE is reportedly using a Palantir database to compile dossiers on protestors
title_fa: ICE is reportedly using a Palantir database to compile dossiers on protestors
excerpt_en: An attorney representing protestors said this infringes on First Amendment rights.
excerpt_fa: An attorney representing protestors said this infringes on First Amendment rights.
content_en:
ICE is reportedly using a Palantir database to compile dossiers on protestors
An attorney representing protestors said this infringes on First Amendment rights.
As revealed by unsealed court documents, Department of Homeland Security agents are allegedly creating dossiers on those that are accused of observing or protesting Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. As first reported by Wired, these DHS files on protestors reportedly include sensitive info like photos and license plate numbers and are stored in a database built by Palantir called Investigative Case Management.
The new information comes from a partially unsealed court filing about a January ICE operation that took place in Maine, according to Wired. The filing is part of a class action lawsuit, which led to a redacted version becoming available to the public on Friday and revealing the purported database of ICE protestors.
According to the lawsuit, DHS agents would track and intimidate observers or protestors, sometimes by driving by their homes or labeling them as "Threat to Law Enforcement, Professional Protestor." In one example, an agent reportedly called one of the plaintiffs on her cell and suggested that she tell her spouse "not to do anything like that in the future because people who are doing things like that might get added to a domestic terrorism watchlist."
The lawyers representing the plaintiffs said that this sort of database creates a chilling effect on the First Amendment rights of protestors. On the other side, a DHS spokesperson told Wired that the case was "meritless" and denied the existence of such a database that labels and tracks "domestic terrorists."

title_en: Federal judge calls Flock ‘indiscriminate mass surveillance’
title_fa: Federal judge calls Flock ‘indiscriminate mass surveillance’
excerpt_en: A federal judge ruled that a sheriff’s deputy violated a woman’s Fourth Amendment rights when using Flock to search for her license plate without a warrant.
excerpt_fa: A federal judge ruled that a sheriff’s deputy violated a woman’s Fourth Amendment rights when using Flock to search for her license plate without a warrant.
content_en:
A federal judge ruled this week that a Tulsa, Oklahoma sheriff’s deputy violated a woman’s Fourth Amendment rights when using Flock Safety to search for her license plate without a warrant.
As reported by 404 Media, this ruling does not create a binding precedent, but it is one of the first times that a federal judge has ruled that a Flock search is unconstitutional.
In this case, Judge Sara Hill said the deputy should have obtained a warrant before searching the Flock database for the woman’s license plate, as he had “no apparent reason” for the search “other than the fact that [the woman’s vehicle] had a California license plate.”
The deputy then used the woman’s travel history in Flock as part of the justification for searching her car, where he allegedly discovered 91 pounds of meth. But Judge Hill wrote that all evidence obtained after the Flock search “must be suppressed as the fruit of a poisonous tree.”
Judge Hill also took broader aim at warrantless searches of the Flock database, writing that tracking people’s location — even when they’re in public places — becomes “constitutionally problematic when law enforcement can indiscriminately and passively catalog your whereabouts over an extended period of time and then use that information for any purpose whenever convenient.”
“This is a type of indiscriminate mass surveillance,” Hill wrote. “It is not targeted on a single individual, as in [Carpenter v. United States, a Supreme Court case focused on how government agencies access location data from cell phones]. It is a tool that collects information about all vehicles that pass by any network-connected camera at all times, and it serves up the information to law enforcement on demand.”
Hill joins a growing chorus of Flock critics from across the political spectrum. Numerous local and state governments, including Florida and Texas, have said they will stop using the technology. And on Friday, Senator Bernie Sanders — a Democrat from Vermont — introduced the Block Flock Act, which would bar federal agencies from using automated license plate readers such as Flock.
Flock CEO Garretty Langley — who we’ll be interviewing on-stage at TechCrunch Disrupt — has called for a “compromise” between privacy and safety and offered an apology to women who have been stalked by law enforcement officers using the Flock system. And with all those cancellations, Flock has also reportedly offered voluntary employee buyouts as a way to shrink its workforce.

title_en: How to check the temperature of your PC's CPU
title_fa: How to check the temperature of your PC's CPU
excerpt_en: There's some solid free software that can help you keep tabs on your computer's health.
excerpt_fa: There's some solid free software that can help you keep tabs on your computer's health.
content_en:
How to check the temperature of your PC's CPU
There's some solid free software that can help you keep tabs on your computer's health.
The temperature of your CPU is one of those things you don't really think about unless something is wrong with your PC. When it's working, this tiny chip makes everything you do on your computer — from having multiple browser tabs open to editing photos and playing your favorite games — run smoothly.
But if your PC is suddenly more sluggish than usual or your fan is starting to sound like a jet engine, there's a good chance it could be overheating and the culprit might be your CPU.
Don't panic! The CPU's temperature can fluctuate for a lot of different reasons, and there are several free tools available that can tell you how it's doing.
Monitoring the temperature of your CPU
One of the best tools you can use to check the temperature of your CPU is HWiNFO, a free diagnostic tool that gives you a ton of real-time data about the hardware in your PC or laptop. Once installed, open the program and click on the Sensors tab to bring up a new window with temperature readings (displayed in Celsius) about your CPU.
There are other free apps like Core Temp and HWMonitor that can provide the same information as well. Whichever you choose, it can be helpful to turn them on every so often to see how your CPU is doing under different conditions. For example, you can fire up a game, video editing software or some other resource-intensive program to see how the CPU temperature changes compared to idle.
While the exact figures vary by CPU, an average running temperature of 60 degrees Celsius or below is typically considered a good baseline for everyday use. But if the CPU is consistently hovering between 70 to 90 degrees Celsius, you should look into what's causing the spike and if it's becoming a long-term problem. Pushing 90 degrees and above could indicate some serious overheating and might reduce the CPU's lifespan if it doesn't cool down.
You'll know ahead of time if it gets to that point: Most modern CPUs will throttle performance once the temperature is too high, significantly slowing down your PC as a way of protecting itself. But if throttling still isn't enough to cool the CPU, you might also experience freezing and crashes.
Keep in mind that these temperature readings are just guidelines and that your experience will vary depending on which CPU model you have. But if you're curious about pushing the limits of your processor (like overclocking for better performance), it's best to consult the original manufacturer for more accurate temperature ranges.
What do you do if it's running hot?
There are a few steps you can take if your CPU is running hotter than normal. It might be as simple as getting rid of a program that's eating up all your processing power — you can test this yourself by opening up Windows Task Manager and closing any apps that could be taxing the CPU.
But if the temperature still doesn't drop, your PC might have more of a hygiene problem than a software one. You can open up your tower to see if any dust has accumulated in the fans or on the components themselves. Use a can of compressed air to push the dust out and improve the airflow in your case. Many cases also have dust filters that can be removed and cleaned out.
You might also need to reapply thermal paste on the CPU, which can dry up over time. The paste serves as a thin layer of connection between the CPU and its heatsink, helping dissipate heat as the temperature rises. This isn't particularly challenging to do yourself, but will require temporarily removing the cooling hardware from your CPU, so find a good guide online and follow along.
The temperature of your CPU is just one indicator of your PC's overall health. But in a time where the price of PCs and laptops have sharply increased due to the AI bubble, it's more important than ever to be proactive about taking care of your electronics.
In addition to GPUs, RAM, and storage, prices of CPUs have been steadily climbing. Earlier this year, both AMD and Intel — two of the biggest chip manufacturers for PCs — increased their CPU prices and reportedly plan on doing it again. So normal check-ups like this can help extend the longevity of your PC and avoid the need to buy costly replacement parts.

title_en: Amazon responds to data center backlash, says it no longer uses NDAs
title_fa: Amazon responds to data center backlash, says it no longer uses NDAs
excerpt_en: The CEO of Amazon Web Services tried to push back against widespread suspicion of data centers.
excerpt_fa: The CEO of Amazon Web Services tried to push back against widespread suspicion of data centers.
content_en:
Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman said the company has stopped using nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) in its dealings with government agencies as it seeks approval to build new data centers.
Garman’s statement is just one sentence in a longer blog post in which he tried to push back against widespread suspicion of data centers, and to make the case that they’re actually good for communities.
NDAs are a significant piece of the broader data center backlash. For example, environmental activist Erin Brockovich recently said that the number one complaint she’s heard about data centers is transparency, with these projects following a common pattern: “projects announced after permits are already secured, developers who don’t return calls, local officials who signed NDAs before their neighbors knew a project was being considered.”
As a result of that backlash, New York announced a one-year moratorium on permits for large data centers, and according to Garman, there are more than 100 data center moratoriums currently being considered across the United States.
“If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman claimed. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”
Garman also attempted to puncture what he said are four big myths around data centers: that they consume too much water, that they increase electricity costs, that they emit an enormous amount of pollution, and that they don’t provide any benefits to their communities.
Pointing to an Amazon report about its own water usage, Garman said that “direct data center water consumption” only accounts for 0.5% of all industrial water usage in the United States, “orders of magnitude less than golf courses, almond farming, and many other industries.”
Nvidia recently said its new cooling system eliminates “pretty much all water usage” inside the data center, but those claims — like Amazon’s — seem to ignore the broader water usage involved in electricity generation and chip manufacturing. Scientists have also said they need to study data centers’ water and energy usage independently, since there are no federal or state requirements around how tech companies report this data.
As for electricity rates, Garman said they’ve only gone up in some states with large numbers of data centers, while they’ve gone down or at least grown more slowly in others. And he argued, “In instances where energy rates are going up, it’s primarily because the grid is old and hasn’t been invested in and expanded before the demand arrived.”
On the other hand, an independent watchdog said recently data centers were the main culprit behind a 76% year-over-year price increase on America’s largest electrical grid.
When it comes to pollution — an issue that the NAACP is currently suing Elon Musk’s SpaceX/xAI over — Garman complained that critics focus on the maximum amount of pollution allowed under data center permits. For example, a planned Amazon data center in Texas is permitted to release 33 million tons of carbon dioxide per year, which is more than any other power plant in the United States.
“The truth is data center generators almost never run,” Garman said. “They’re idle 99.9% of the time (they run roughly 10 hours per year, mostly for required maintenance testing).”
As for the community benefits, this is where Garman wrote, “We no longer use nondisclosure agreements with the government agencies we work with on our projects.” Plus, he said, “Over the past three years, Amazon has contributed more than $1 billion to communities across the U.S. in which we have a meaningful data center presence.”
Will this be enough to quell community suspicion? Perhaps not — Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently argued that the AI backlash is “fundamentally a crisis of trust,” where people assume governments and tech companies are always “cooking up some new way to screw them over.” Similarly, writer Jasmine Sun noted that when data center opponents are presented with the tech companies’ arguments, their response is usually, “I don’t believe them.”
